Chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates and a physical exam reveals mild crackles. Which of the following is the least likely causative agent of this patient's condition?
questions.solution: The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Atypical pneumonia or walking pneumonia due to the mild symptoms and the ability to continue daily activities despite the infection. questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient is scheduled for an MRI to evaluate cognitive changes. Which of the following systems is specifically designed to provide shielding against radio frequency interference during the scan?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient is scheduled for an MRI to evaluate cognitive changes. Which of the following systems is specifically designed to provide shielding against radio frequency interference during the scan?
questions.solution: A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure that shields its inner space from electromagnetic interference. In MRI environments, this enclosure is typically constructed using wooden panels wrapped in copper wires, which provide effective radiofrequency (RF) shielding. This shielding helps minimize interference, which leads to imaging artifacts and ensures clearer and more accurate MRI results. In the MRI facility, the cage is often visible through the special window glass separating the control room from the scanner area, further emphasizing its role in maintaining optimal imaging conditions. Gradient Coils (Option A) are three sets, X, Y, and Z, used in the MRI imaging process to create intentional variations in the main magnetic field. These changes in the magnetic field enable the localisation of image slices. Helmholtz coils (Option B) are a pair of circular coils arranged parallel to one another and function as Z gradient coils in MRI scanners. Shim coils (Option C) are used to correct minor spatial discrepancies in the main static magnetic field and ensure optimal spatial uniformity, improving MRI image quality by reducing artifacts. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male patient with a history of severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for elective hip replacement surgery. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for general anesthesia in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male patient with a history of severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for elective hip replacement surgery. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for general anesthesia in this patient?
questions.solution: Patient refusal is an absolute contraindication for general anesthesia in this patient. General anesthesia General anesthesia induces unconsciousness and blocks pain while controlling autonomic reflexes. Main anesthetic agents: IV anesthetics Inhalational anesthetics IV sedatives Synthetic opioids Neuromuscular blocking drugs. Common process: IV sedatives and analgesics for induction, followed by volatile anesthetics for maintenance. Absolute contraindication : Patient refusal. (Option A) Relative contraindications : Unoptimized medical conditions, difficult airway or significant comorbidities (e.g., severe aortic stenosis, pulmonary disease, CHF), procedures better suited for regional or neuraxial anesthesia to avoid airway manipulation. (Option B & C ruled out) Common side effects: Transient confusion or memory loss Dizziness Urinary retention Nausea and vomiting Chills Sore throat. Mallampati class IV airway (Option C): Mallampati class III and IV indicate a difficult airway during intubation, and thus a relative contraindication of general anesthesia @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Patient refusal is an absolute contraindication for general anesthesia in this patient.

 

General anesthesia
  • General anesthesia induces unconsciousness and blocks pain while controlling autonomic reflexes.
  • Main anesthetic agents:
    • IV anesthetics
    • Inhalational anesthetics
    • IV sedatives
    • Synthetic opioids
    • Neuromuscular blocking drugs.
  • Common process: IV sedatives and analgesics for induction, followed by volatile anesthetics for maintenance.
  • Absolute contraindication: Patient refusal. (Option A)
  • Relative contraindications: Unoptimized medical conditions, difficult airway or significant comorbidities (e.g., severe aortic stenosis, pulmonary disease, CHF), procedures better suited for regional or neuraxial anesthesia to avoid airway manipulation. (Option B & C ruled out)
  • Common side effects:
    • Transient confusion or memory loss
    • Dizziness
    • Urinary retention
    • Nausea and vomiting
    • Chills
    • Sore throat.

 

Mallampati class IV airway (Option C): Mallampati class III and IV indicate a difficult airway during intubation, and thus a relative contraindication of general anesthesia

Which of the following statements regarding this test is correct?
questions.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student presents to the clinic with a 2-week history of fatigue, sore throat, fever, and swollen lymph nodes. On examination, he has significant posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. The physician suspects a viral infection and decides to perform a specific agglutination test. Which of the following statements regarding this test is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The test detects heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep red blood cells.

options.label: B
options.text: An agglutination titer of 50 or below is indicative of a positive result.

options.label: C
options.text: The test requires fresh serum samples without any prior heating.

options.label: D
options.text: Heterophile antibodies are produced only in response to one type of virus

questions.answerText: The test detects heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep red blood cells.
questions.solution: with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test , which detects heterophile IgM antibodies . These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells —a hallmark of EBV infection. Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests: Weil-Felix : Rickettsial infections Paul-Bunnell : Infectious mononucleosis Cold agglutination : Mycoplasma pneumonia Streptococcus MG : Streptococcal antibodies Paul-Bunnell Test Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV. Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum. Principle : Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections Procedure : Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs Interpretation : Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection Note : Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

  • Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test, which detects heterophile IgM antibodies. These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells—a hallmark of EBV infection.

    • Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests:

    • Weil-Felix: Rickettsial infections

    • Paul-Bunnell: Infectious mononucleosis

    • Cold agglutination: Mycoplasma pneumonia

    • Streptococcus MG: Streptococcal antibodies

    Paul-Bunnell Test

    • Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV.
    • Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum.

    • Principle: Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections

    • Procedure: Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs

    • Interpretation: Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection

    • Note: Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the jaw jerk reflex is false?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about the jaw jerk reflex is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a spinal reflex initiated by tapping the jaw.

options.label: B
options.text: It involves the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus as an integration centre.

options.label: C
options.text: The efferent pathway includes the mandibular nerve.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a monosynaptic reflex involving a single synapse.

questions.answerText: It is a spinal reflex initiated by tapping the jaw.
questions.solution: he jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw. Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex It is a deep tendon reflex. The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid). The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles. Afferent pathway: Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Integration centre (Relay): Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out) Efferent pathway: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out) This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw. The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out) The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
he jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw.

 

Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex

It is a deep tendon reflex.

  • The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid).
  • The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles.
  • Afferent pathway: Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Integration centre (Relay): Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out)
  • Efferent pathway: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out)
  • This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw.
  • The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out)
  • The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways.

questions.solution: rio, the patient presents with signs and symptoms of intraperitoneal bladder rupture, which is a surgical emergency. Therefore, emergency laparotomy is done immediately. Intraperitoneal rupture Involves a tear or injury to the peritoneum over the bladder, and urine leaks into the peritoneal cavity in males. Causes: Often occurs in a fully distended bladder, usually due to trauma or injury. Clinical Features: Sudden, severe pain in the suprapubic region. Signs of shock and syncope. The contrast outlines the bowel loops. Ultrasound: To assess other abdominal injuries. {{caption_text}} Treatment: Emergency Laparotomy is required. (Option B). Complications: Cystitis /and pyelonephritis. Peritonitis. Pelvic abscess. Fistula formation (vesicovaginal or rectovesical). Paralytic ileus. Hemorrhage. tion:

The X-ray shows a lung abscess. Aspiration is the most common cause of lung abscesses, particularly in the apical lower lobe, and is frequently associated with anaerobic bacteria from the oral cavity.

 

Lung Abscess Localized suppuration in the lung is characterized by tissue necrosis

 

Aetiology:

  • Infectious: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus, anaerobic bacteria, etc.
  • Chronic upper respiratory infections (e.g., sinusitis, tonsillitis, dental infections).
  • Mechanical: Bronchial obstruction due to tumours or foreign bodies.
  • Other Causes: Septicaemia and aspiration, commonly lead to lung abscess in the apical lower lobe.

Sites of Infection:

  • Apical Lower Lobe: Most frequently involved in aspiration-related lung abscesses.
  • Posterior Segments: Can be affected due to gravity when aspiration occurs.
  • Upper Lobes: May be involved in cases of tuberculosis or certain types of pneumonia.

 

Routes of Infection:

  • Aspiration: Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastrointestinal secretions, often leading to anaerobic infections from the oral cavity.
  • Hematogenous Spread: From e.g., endocarditis or septicemia
  • Direct Extension: Localized infections in adjacent structures (e.g., pneumonia, empyema) can extend into lung tissue.

 

 

Hematogenous spread from endocarditis (Option B): While it can cause lung abscesses, it is less common than aspiration in the context of anaerobic infections and would typically present with multiple abscesses rather than a localized opacity.

Direct extension from pneumonia (Option C) can cause lung abscesses, but in this case, the specific presence of anaerobic bacteria and the apical location suggest aspiration as the more likely cause.

Bronchial obstruction due to lung cancer (Option D) is a possible cause of infection and abscess formation, but the presence of anaerobic bacteria and the patient's age make aspiration a more plausible cause, especially in the context of a localized opacity in the lung.

diagnosis in this clinical presentation is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion disease.

 

Prion Disease or Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathy (TSE):

  • Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles with no RNA/DNA.
  • Pathogenesis: Misfolding of normal prion protein (PrPc) to form beta-pleated configuration (PrPSc).
  • Histopathology: Spongiform vacuolisation inside the cell.
  • Associated diseases:

Types of prion disease
1. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (M/C)

  • Genetic: Familial form caused by PRNP mutation.
  • Transmission: Iatrogenic
  • Symptoms:
    • Dementia.

  • Histopathogenesis:
    • Spongiform transformation of the cerebral cortex.
  • Prognosis: Uniformly fatal with average survival < 7 months after the onset of symptoms.

2. Kuru disease

  • PAS & Congo: red positive.
  • Kuru plaques: Extracellular aggregated abnormal PrP.

3. Fatal familial insomnia

4. Bovine spongiform encephalopathy

Explanation:

  • The Eustachian tube regulates air pressure in the middle ear by allowing air exchange between the ear and the nasopharynx.
  • When the tube is blocked, often due to inflammation from a respiratory infection, oxygen and the other gases in the middle ear are absorbed, creating negative pressure.
  • This leads to the retraction of the tympanic membrane and fluid buildup behind it, which explains the patient's symptoms.

 

Barotrauma from rapid pressure changes (Option A): Barotrauma occurs when there is a sudden change in air pressure, such as during aeroplane takeoff or diving. The rapid pressure shift can cause ear pain and tympanic membrane damage. In this case, however, there is no history of exposure to such conditions.

 

Increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (Option B): Allergic reactions can lead to hyperactivity of the mucosa lining the middle ear, resulting in fluid accumulation. However, this typically presents with other signs of allergic response, such as itching or sneezing, and is not as strongly associated with a recent cold as Eustachian tube dysfunction.


Biofilm formation in the middle ear (Option C): Biofilm formation is associated with chronic conditions and resistance to treatment, but this patient's symptoms are more acute.

Hypothermia

Definition

Hypothermia is defined as a drop in core body temperature below 35°C, resulting in the failure to maintain homeostasis and affecting all organ systems.

Types
  • Primary Hypothermia: Caused by environmental cold exposure, such as cold air or water. Common in cold geographic areas but can also occur in mild climates.
  • Secondary Hypothermia: Results from conditions that impair heat production or increase heat loss (e.g., trauma, burns, drug overdoses, endocrine disorders, CNS injury, or drug effects).

Clinical Features

Mild Hypothermia (32-35°C / 90-95°F)

(Option A)

  • Symptoms: Hunger, nausea, fatigue, shivering, pale/dry skin, increased muscle tone, blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration.
  • Neurologic symptoms: Cognitive decline, memory impairment, ataxia, dysarthria.
  • Shivering may stop if energy stores are depleted (e.g., malnutrition).
  • Cold-induced diuresis due to peripheral vasoconstriction.

Moderate Hypothermia (28-32°C / 82-90°F)

(Option B)
  • Cognitive decline, lethargy, CNS depression (hyporeflexia, dilated pupils).
  • Shivering stops at 30-32°C.
  • Paradoxical undressing may occur.
  • Increased risk of atrial fibrillation, hypotension, bradycardia, bradypnea.

Severe Hypothermia (<28°C / <82°F)

(Option C)
  • Unresponsiveness, further decline in cerebral blood flow, hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac output.
  • Risk of atrial, junctional dysrhythmias.
  • Pulmonary congestion, oliguria, and areflexia.
  • Potential for cardiorespiratory failure and death.

ECG Findings
  • Atrial Fibrillation: Most common arrhythmia in hypothermic patients.
  • Bradycardia: Seen in moderate to severe hypothermia, increasing the risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
  • QT Interval Prolongation: Due to slowed impulse conduction through potassium channels.
  • Osborn (J) Waves: Elevated J point, visible on ECG in the precordial leads, with wave height proportional to the degree of hypothermia.

questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old male presents to the clinic with worsening dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and ankle swelling. He has a past medical history of chronic heart failure, which was diagnosed 5 years ago. Despite being on several medications, he continues to experience symptoms. On examination, his heart rate is irregular and there is evidence of jugular venous distension. What is the drug of choice for managing his condition?
questions.solution: cardiac glycoside, is commonly used to manage chronic heart failure with atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response. It helps control heart rate and improve symptoms in patients with atrial fibrillation. Digoxin at therapeutic concentrations mildly inhibits the cardiac Na + /K + ATPase, causing an increase in intracellular Na + . Increased Na + inhibits Ca 2+ extrusion via the NCX, resulting in higher intracellular Ca 2+ and enhanced contractility. The increased contractility and cardiac output provide symptomatic relief (primarily in systolic dysfunction) in patients with heart failure. When the main trigger for neurohumoral activation is removed, sympathetic nerve tone, heart rate, and peripheral vascular resistance drop. The decrease in preload and afterload reduces chamber dilation and wall stress. Increased renal perfusion lowers renin production and increases diuresis, further decreasing preload. Lisinopril (Option A) is an ACE inhibitor used in heart failure, but does not directly address the patient's atrial fibrillation or rapid ventricular response. Carvedilol (Option B) is a beta-blocker used in heart failure but does not specifically target atrial fibrillation. Furosemide (Option C) is a loop diuretic that manages fluid overload in heart failure but does not address the patient's arrhythmia. @Neet_pg_bot

Consistency of the association E. Biological plausibility F. Coherence of the association Descriptions: 1. Requires that exposure precedes the onset of a disease. 2. Based on relative risk and dose-response relationship. 3. Implies a "one-to-one" relationship between cause and effect. 4. Replication of results in different settings strengthens evidence. 5. questions.stemHtml:
Match the following criteria for judging causality with their descriptions:
Criteria:
A. Temporal association
B. Strength of association
C. Specificity of the association
D. Consistency of the association
E. Biological plausibility
F. Coherence of the association
Descriptions:
1. Requires that exposure precedes the onset of a disease.
2. Based on relative risk and dose-response relationship.
3. Implies a "one-to-one" relationship between cause and effect.
4. Replication of results in different settings strengthens evidence.
5. Agreement with current understanding of biological response.
6. Consistency with known relevant facts.
questions.solution: rd Hill gives a few criteria on which the relationship between disease and cause increases. Hill’s criteria: Temporality The cause must precede the observed effect. In chronic diseases, establishing temporal sequence can be challenging due to insidious onset and ignorance of precise induction periods. Example: Lung cancer occurring in long-term smokers satisfies the temporal requirement. Strength Relative risk and dose-response relationship are assessed. A larger relative risk strengthens the likelihood of causal association. The biological gradient or dose-response relationship reinforces the causal relationship. Cessation experiments, like reduction in mortality ratios after quitting smoking, provide evidence for causality. Specificity Implies a "one-to-one" relationship between cause and effect. Lack of specificity does not negate the causal hypothesis. Multiple diseases associated with a single factor do not necessarily disprove causality. Example: Although smoking is associated with various diseases, the association with lung cancer is predominant. Consistency Replication of results in different settings and by different methods strengthens evidence. Example: More than 50 retrospective studies and numerous prospective studies globally have shown a consistent association between smoking and lung cancer. Plausibility The association agrees with the current understanding of the biological response. The lack of biological mechanisms does not rule out causality. Example: Inhalation of smoke leading to deposition of carcinogens in the lungs is biologically plausible. Coherence Consistency with known facts relevant to the association. Historical evidence of rising tobacco consumption and lung cancer incidence. Differences in trends of lung cancer death rates between genders coherent with smoking patterns. Fall in lung cancer risk upon smoking cessation and increase in risk with occupational exposure to carcinogens reinforce the causal association. Analogy If a similar association has been observed with another exposure and outcome, it supports the possibility of a causal relationship. Gradient There should be a direct relationship between the dose of the exposure and the risk of the disease. Higher levels of exposure should lead to higher incidences of the disease. Experiment Evidence obtained from experimental studies, particularly randomised controlled trials, that manipulate the exposure and observe the effect on the outcome can provide strong support for causation. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
rd Hill gives a few criteria on which the relationship between disease and cause increases.

Hill’s criteria:

Temporality
  • The cause must precede the observed effect.
  • In chronic diseases, establishing temporal sequence can be challenging due to insidious onset and ignorance of precise induction periods.
  • Example: Lung cancer occurring in long-term smokers satisfies the temporal requirement.

Strength
  • Relative risk and dose-response relationship are assessed.
  • A larger relative risk strengthens the likelihood of causal association.
  • The biological gradient or dose-response relationship reinforces the causal relationship.
  • Cessation experiments, like reduction in mortality ratios after quitting smoking, provide evidence for causality.

Specificity
  • Implies a "one-to-one" relationship between cause and effect.
  • Lack of specificity does not negate the causal hypothesis.
  • Multiple diseases associated with a single factor do not necessarily disprove causality.
  • Example: Although smoking is associated with various diseases, the association with lung cancer is predominant.

Consistency
  • Replication of results in different settings and by different methods strengthens evidence.
  • Example: More than 50 retrospective studies and numerous prospective studies globally have shown a consistent association between smoking and lung cancer.

Plausibility
  • The association agrees with the current understanding of the biological response.
  • The lack of biological mechanisms does not rule out causality.
  • Example: Inhalation of smoke leading to deposition of carcinogens in the lungs is biologically plausible.

Coherence
  • Consistency with known facts relevant to the association.
  • Historical evidence of rising tobacco consumption and lung cancer incidence.
  • Differences in trends of lung cancer death rates between genders coherent with smoking patterns.
  • Fall in lung cancer risk upon smoking cessation and increase in risk with occupational exposure to carcinogens reinforce the causal association.

Analogy
  • If a similar association has been observed with another exposure and outcome, it supports the possibility of a causal relationship.

Gradient
  • There should be a direct relationship between the dose of the exposure and the risk of the disease.
  • Higher levels of exposure should lead to higher incidences of the disease.

Experiment
  • Evidence obtained from experimental studies, particularly randomised controlled trials, that manipulate the exposure and observe the effect on the outcome can provide strong support for causation.

questions.solution: Calcitonin is a hormone produced by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland that plays a crucial role in regulating calcium homeostasis. Calcitonin:

  • A hormone produced by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland.

ppocampus plays no role in depressive disorders

 

Explanation:

Brain dysfunctions affecting the amygdala, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex are factors that lead to depressive disorder in many cases.

 

Epidemiology of Depressive Disorders:

  • General trend: Prevalence increases with age.
    • Females > males (Children: Boys = Girls).
    • Mean age of onset (40 yrs)
    • May be more common in Rural > Urban areas
    • Low socio-economic status > High socio-economic status
    • 20% experience major depression by age 18.
  • Family History: ~3 times higher risks if a first-degree relative has major depression.
  • Persistent Depressive Disorder/Dysthymia/Dysthymic Disorder: According to DSM-5, persistent depressive disorder is diagnosed when depressive symptoms persist for 2 or more years (or 1 year for children), with no symptom-free periods lasting longer than 2 months during the illness.
  • Double Depression: ~9.9% develop major depression within 6 months of persistent depressive disorder.

 

Etiology of Depressive Disorders:

 

Environmental factors

Biological factors
  • Acute negative life events
    • Many cases are preceded by such events
    • Loss of a significant person or relation like a spouse
    • Immigrant or refugees due to loss, isolation, and trauma of migration
       
  • Chronic stress: Poverty, unemployment, single motherhood, poor housing, poor residential conditions, parents of disabled children
     
  • Childhood adversity: Early exposure to trauma (loss of a parent)
     
  • Social and institutional barriers: Racism, discrimination, and socioeconomic status
  • Monoamine hypothesis: deficiency or dysregulation of brain monoamines leads to depressive symptoms (Option B)
     
  • Neuroendocrine:
    • HPA axis hyperactivity
    • Hypercortisolemia
    • Undetected thyroid dysfunction
    • Low brain-derived neurotropic factor
       
  • Neurotransmitter deficits:
    • Norepinephrine: decreased sensitivity of beta-adrenergic receptors
    • Low serotonin precipitates depression
    • Dopamine may be reduced
    • Decreased GABA levels due to chronic stress
    • Decreased 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA)
    • Increased level of ACh and glutamate.
       
  • Brain dysfunction affecting the amygdala, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex
     
  • Neurogenesis hypothesis stating brain abnormalities causing depression is due to developmental anomalies leading to a deficiency of neurons (Option A)
     
  • Neuroplasticity hypothesis states that the atrophy of already-developed neurons can cause depression (Option C)
  • Immune system processes
    • Chronic stress may activate immune responses (CRF, cytokines, and interleukins), leading to inflammation.
    • Elevated proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, CRP), indicate a bidirectional relationship between depression and inflammatory responses.
       
  • Genetic vulnerability
    • Family history significantly increases risk.

ith halothane-induced hepatitis, also known as Type-2 halothane hepatotoxicity. This is an immune-mediated reaction that typically occurs 1-2 weeks after exposure to halothane, especially in patients with previous exposure or risk factors such as moderate alcohol use.

Halothane

Category

Details

Chemical Properties

- Clear, heavy, colorless liquid

- Sweet, non-irritating odor, photosensitive (stored in an amber bottle with thymol preservative)

- Structure of an alkane

- Highly soluble in blood and tissues, hence can cause delayed recovery

Systemic Effects

- Cardiovascular: Myocardial depression, sensitization to catecholamines

- Respiratory: Respiratory depression

- Central Nervous System: General anesthesia, increased cerebral blood flow

Uses

- Induction and maintenance of general anesthesia

- Less commonly used now due to side effect profile

- Still used in some resource-limited settings

Side Effects

- Type 1 Hepatotoxicity: Mild, self-limiting liver injury (20-30% of patients)

- Type 2 Hepatotoxicity (Halothane Hepatitis): Severe, potentially fatal (1 in 35,000 after single exposure)

- Cardiorespiratory instability

- Arrhythmias, especially in children

- Malignant hyperthermia (rare)

Metabolism

- 20-45% metabolized in the liver

- Produces trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protein adducts which are immunogenic and are responsible for causing halothane hepatitis.

pH: 7.43, PaCO₂: 38 mmHg, PaO₂: 54 mmHg, HCO₃⁻: 24 mEq/L.

questions.solution: Correct answer is B: Increase Fio2 The patient has Type 1 respiratory failure (low PaO₂ with normal PaCO₂), indicating a pure oxygenation problem . Increasing FiO₂ is the most direct and effective way to raise PaO₂.It is alos the lastest and simplest way to improve oxygenation. It provides immediate increase in alveolar oxygen concentration and thus raises PaO₂ quickly. Always titrate FiO₂ up to 60% (0.6) before increasing PEEP. Increasing tidal volume (A) or minute ventilation (D) would reduce CO₂, not help oxygenation. Decreasing RR (C) would worsen oxygenation by lowering minute ventilation and overall alveolar exposure to oxygen. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: tomMeta" data-dictid="a5c6cb079d16927771967e62ffee72">posterior mediastinum. Infections in this space can easily spread to the mediastinum, leading to mediastinitis . Classification of Spaces: Suprahyoid spaces: Located above the hyoid bone, including the submandibular and prevertebral spaces. Infrahyoid spaces: Located below the hyoid bone, typically related to deeper neck structures. Suprahyoid spaces: Submental space Deep to upper investing layer of deep cervical fascia, superficial to mylohyoid muscles Submandibular space Deep to the concerned half of the mandible, between the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle Sublingual space Deep to mylohyoid muscles in the floor of the mouth, continuous with the opposite side Peritonsillar space Part of intrapharyngeal space, around palatine tonsils between pillars of fauces Parapharyngeal space On either side of the posterolateral aspect of pharynx Medially - superior constrictor of pharynx Laterally - medial pterygoid Retropharyngeal space Anteriorly - buccopharyngeal fascia of pharynx Posteriorly - prevertebral layer Laterally - carotid sheath Superiorly - cranial base Infrahyoid Spaces: Pretracheal space Behind pretracheal fascia and infrahyoid muscles, in front of the anterior wall of esophagus. Retrovisceral space Between the posterior wall of pharynx/esophagus and prevertebral fascia. Prevertebral space Between prevertebral fascia and vertebral column. Carotid space Around the contents of carotid sheath, demarcated by parts of investing, pretracheal, and prevertebral layers. Parapharyngeal space (Option A): While this space is adjacent to the pharynx and can be a site of infection, it does not communicate directly with the mediastinum. Carotid space (Option B): This space contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve but is not typically involved in spreading infections to the mediastinum. Prevertebral space (Option D): Infections here can affect the vertebrae or muscles but are less likely to spread to the mediastinum compared to the retropharyngeal space. @Neet_pg_bot

tomMeta" data-dictid="a5c6cb079d16927771967e62ffee72">posterior mediastinum. Infections in this space can easily spread to the mediastinum, leading to mediastinitis.

 

Classification of Spaces:

  • Suprahyoid spaces: Located above the hyoid bone, including the submandibular and prevertebral spaces.
  • Infrahyoid spaces: Located below the hyoid bone, typically related to deeper neck structures.

 

Suprahyoid spaces:

 

Submental space
  • Deep to upper investing layer of deep cervical fascia, superficial to mylohyoid muscles

Submandibular space
  • Deep to the concerned half of the mandible, between the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle

Sublingual space
  • Deep to mylohyoid muscles in the floor of the mouth, continuous with the opposite side

Peritonsillar space
  • Part of intrapharyngeal space, around palatine tonsils between pillars of fauces

Parapharyngeal space
  • On either side of the posterolateral aspect of pharynx
  • Medially - superior constrictor of pharynx
  • Laterally - medial pterygoid

Retropharyngeal space
  • Anteriorly - buccopharyngeal fascia of pharynx
  • Posteriorly - prevertebral layer
  • Laterally - carotid sheath
  • Superiorly - cranial base

 

Infrahyoid Spaces:

 

Pretracheal space
  • Behind pretracheal fascia and infrahyoid muscles, in front of the anterior wall of esophagus.

Retrovisceral space
  • Between the posterior wall of pharynx/esophagus and prevertebral fascia.

Prevertebral space
  • Between prevertebral fascia and vertebral column.

Carotid space
  • Around the contents of carotid sheath, demarcated by parts of investing, pretracheal, and prevertebral layers.

Parapharyngeal space (Option A): While this space is adjacent to the pharynx and can be a site of infection, it does not communicate directly with the mediastinum.
 

Carotid space (Option B): This space contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve but is not typically involved in spreading infections to the mediastinum.
 

Prevertebral space (Option D): Infections here can affect the vertebrae or muscles but are less likely to spread to the mediastinum compared to the retropharyngeal space.

The patient is a typical case of Budd-Chiari like Syndrome, a type of Veno Occlusive Disease (VOD) commonly seen in the patients on busulfan. Warfarin is an anticoagulant and is not used for the treatment of VOD. Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

Side effects of Busulfan includes:-

  • Bone marrow suppression (maximum risk)
  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • Seizures
  • Budd-Chiari like syndrome
  • Tumor lysis syndrome

The patient’s should be started on defibrotide as the symptoms are likely due to Budd-Chiari syndrome (Veno-Occlusive Disease) (Option A):

The management of VOD focuses on use of defibrotide which is an antithrombotic agent as the treatment of choice.

 

Patients should be started on antiepileptics such as phenytoin to prevent seizures (Option C):

Patients on Busulfan, if experiencing episodes of seizures, are to be started on phenytoin, which is the frequently used anti-epileptic for patients on Busulfan. However, Phenytoin also induces the enzymes that metabolize busulfan, reducing its plasma concentration by about 20% thus reducing its side effects.

 

Adjust the dose of busulfan based on plasma drug-level monitoring (Option D):

 

Adjusting the dose of Busulfan based on plasma drug-level monitoring is frequently done to balance therapeutic efficacy and minimize toxicity, especially since Busulfan clearance can vary significantly among patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is most important in the impedance-matching mechanism of the auditory system, facilitating the transfer of sound from the air-filled middle ear to the fluid-filled cochlea?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following factors is most important in the impedance-matching mechanism of the auditory system, facilitating the transfer of sound from the air-filled middle ear to the fluid-filled cochlea?

options.label: A
options.text: Acoustic Reflex of the Middle Ear Muscles

options.label: B
options.text: Area ratio between the tympanic membrane and the oval window

options.label: C
options.text: Lever action of the malleus and stapes

questions.answerText: Area ratio between the tympanic membrane and the oval window
questions.solution: > Explanation: The impedance-matching mechanism ensures efficient sound transmission from the air-filled middle ear to the fluid-filled cochlea. The tympanic membrane has a much larger surface area than the stapes footplate at the oval window. This area ratio, approximately 14:1, amplifies the sound pressure by concentrating the vibrations from a large surface (tympanic membrane) to a smaller one (oval window). This is the most significant contributor to impedance matching. The middle ear serves as an impedance-matching transformer, increasing the pressure of sound waves to overcome this mismatch. There are three key mechanisms involved in this process: Mechanism Description Function Lever Action of the Ossicles (Option C ruled out) The malleus has a longer handle compared to the incus , forming a lever system. Amplifies vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the stapes footplate by a factor of 1.3. Hydraulic Action of the Tympanic Membrane The tympanic membrane is larger than the stapes footplate, with an area ratio of about 21:1, reduced to 14:1 due to functional area. Concentrates force at the smaller stapes footplate, significantly increasing sound pressure. Curved Membrane Effect The tympanic membrane is slightly conical, causing greater vibrations at the periphery than at the centre. Increases the force applied to the ossicles, enhancing sound energy transmission. Acoustic Reflex of the Middle Ear Muscles (Option A) : Contraction of the stapedius and tensor tympani muscles in response to loud sounds reduces the amplitude of sound transmission but does not significantly contribute to impedance matching. Resonance of the basilar membrane (Option D) plays a role in frequency discrimination within the cochlea but is not part of the impedance-matching process in the middle ear. @Neet_pg_bot

Type of Cyst

Description

Details

Functional Cyst

Fluid-filled sacs that form on the ovaries, typically during the menstrual cycle.

  •  2 Types:
    1. Follicular cysts form due to hormonal dysfunction prior to ovulation, leading to expansion of the follicular antrum with serous fluid.
    2. Corpus luteum cysts form due to excessive hemorrhage from the vascular corpus luteum following ovulation.
  • High-dose combination oral contraceptives (COCs) suppress ovarian activity and protect against cyst development.
  • Surgical excision is considered for large, persistent cysts or smaller ones causing persistent symptoms. Usually benign and not cancerous.

Gartner’s Cyst

Forms from remnants of the Wolffian duct

  • Located along vaginal walls
  • Can cause discomfort, urinary issues, or dyspareunia if large
  • Treatment may involve surgical removal if symptomatic

Skene’s Cyst

Located near the urethra in females, formed from the Skene’s glands.

  • Involved in lubrication of the urethral opening. Usually presents as a urethral diverticulum.
  • Cysts here can cause urinary problems, pain, or discomfort.
  • Treatment may include antibiotics for infection or surgical drainage/removal if necessary.

Nabothian Cyst

Mucus-filled cysts that occur on the cervix.

  • Form when mucus-producing glands in the cervix are covered by skin cells, trapping the mucus.
  • Generally harmless, asymptomatic and often found during routine pelvic exams.
  • No treatment is typically required unless they cause significant symptoms, in which case they can be drained or removed.

questions.stemHtml: In the His bundle electrogram (HBE), what does the H wave denote?
questions.solution: a" data-dictid="dbaf58dd301692777186f2a8d7b3a0">depolarization of the His bundle His Bundle Electrogram (HBE): Invasive ECG procedure A catheter containing an electrode at its tip is inserted through an arm vein into the right atrium close to the tricuspid valve. The electrode records the HBE. Waveforms in the His Bundle Electrogram A Wave (Option A) The A wave represents atrial depolarization. H Wave (Option C) The H wave represents depolarization of the His bundle’s upper part. V Wave: (Option B) The V wave represents ventricular depolarization. Intervals in the His Bundle Electrogram P-A Interval The PA interval is the time from the onset of the P wave on the surface ECG to the onset of the A wave on the His bundle electrogram. The PA interval typically ranges from 25 to 55 milliseconds. A-H Interval The A-H interval is the time between the onset of the A wave and the onset of the H wave. Typically ranges from 50 to 120 milliseconds. This interval represents conduction time through the AV node. A prolonged A-H interval suggests AV nodal conduction delay. H-V Interval Typically ranges from 35 to 55 milliseconds. This interval represents conduction time through the His-Purkinje system. A prolonged H-V interval suggests an infranodal conduction delay or block. @Neet_pg_bot

a" data-dictid="dbaf58dd301692777186f2a8d7b3a0">depolarization of the His bundle

His Bundle Electrogram (HBE):

  • Invasive ECG procedure
  • A catheter containing an electrode at its tip is inserted through an arm vein into the right atrium close to the tricuspid valve. The electrode records the HBE.

 

 

Waveforms in the His Bundle Electrogram
 

A Wave

(Option A)

The A wave represents atrial depolarization.
 

H Wave

(Option C)

The H wave represents depolarization of the His bundle’s upper part.
 

V Wave:

(Option B)

The V wave represents ventricular depolarization.
 

Intervals in the His Bundle Electrogram
 

P-A Interval
  • The PA interval is the time from the onset of the P wave on the surface ECG to the onset of the A wave on the His bundle electrogram.
  • The PA interval typically ranges from 25 to 55 milliseconds.
 

A-H Interval
  • The A-H interval is the time between the onset of the A wave and the onset of the H wave.
  • Typically ranges from 50 to 120 milliseconds.
  • This interval represents conduction time through the AV node. A prolonged A-H interval suggests AV nodal conduction delay.
 

H-V Interval
  • Typically ranges from 35 to 55 milliseconds.
  • This interval represents conduction time through the His-Purkinje system. A prolonged H-V interval suggests an infranodal conduction delay or block.

questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with confusion, tremors, and diaphoresis. He has a long history of chronic alcohol use and has been drinking heavily for the past week. His family reports that he has not eaten well during this time. Upon examination, you note signs of malnutrition and his blood glucose level is found to be 50 mg/dL.
Which of the following statements regarding the effects of chronic alcoholism on nutritional deficiencies and blood glucose levels is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic alcohol use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency despite normal blood levels.

options.label: B
options.text: Folate deficiency in alcoholics leads to megaloblastic anemia.

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

questions.answerText: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.
questions.solution: Correct answer : D) Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Chronic alcohol use and metabolism: Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, shifting metabolic pathways. Excess NADH promotes the conversion of pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting key gluconeogenic precursors. This inhibits gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, especially in malnourished individuals. The false statement is Option D , which states that alcohol decreases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which is incorrect . Alcohol-Induced Metabolic Effects and Nutritional Deficiencies Effect Mechanism Increased NADH/NAD+ Ratio (Option C ruled out) Alcohol metabolism (via alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) generates excess NADH, disrupting metabolic pathways. Hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out) Excess NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis, contributing to hypoglycemia. Pyruvate and oxaloacetate are diverted to lactate and malate, depleting gluconeogenic substrates. Lactic Acidosis Excess NADH promotes pyruvate to lactate conversion. Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Option A ruled out) Alcohol impairs B12 absorption despite normal blood levels. Folate Deficiency (Option B ruled out) Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and storage, leading to megaloblastic anemia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer : D) Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

  • Chronic alcohol use and metabolism:

    • Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, shifting metabolic pathways.

    • Excess NADH promotes the conversion of pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting key gluconeogenic precursors.

    • This inhibits gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, especially in malnourished individuals.

    • The false statement is Option D, which states that alcohol decreases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which is incorrect.

Alcohol-Induced Metabolic Effects and Nutritional Deficiencies

Effect Mechanism
Increased NADH/NAD+ Ratio (Option C ruled out) Alcohol metabolism (via alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) generates excess NADH, disrupting metabolic pathways.
Hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out) Excess NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis, contributing to hypoglycemia. Pyruvate and oxaloacetate are diverted to lactate and malate, depleting gluconeogenic substrates.
Lactic Acidosis Excess NADH promotes pyruvate to lactate conversion.
Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Option A ruled out) Alcohol impairs B12 absorption despite normal blood levels.
Folate Deficiency (Option B ruled out) Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and storage, leading to megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: Gold standard investigation for steatorrhea is?
questions.stemHtml: Gold standard investigation for steatorrhea is?
questions.solution: Correct answer is A: 72-hour faecal fat estimation Steatorrhea is defined as stool fat excretion > 7% fat of dietary fat. Gold standard investigation for it is 72-hour faecal fat estimation. Breath triolein test is a non-invasive screening method but not the gold standard; it’s less sensitive and rarely used in clinical practice. Correct answer is A: 72-hour faecal fat estimation

  • Steatorrhea is defined as stool fat excretion > 7% fat of dietary fat. Gold standard investigation for it is 72-hour faecal fat estimation.
  • Breath triolein test is a non-invasive screening method but not the gold standard; it’s less sensitive and rarely used in clinical practice.
  • PIVKA test measures abnormal prothrombin due to vitamin K deficiency, mainly used as a marker for liver cancer
  • Small intestinal mucosal biopsy is useful for identifying underlying mucosal diseases (like celiac disease) causing malabsorption, but it does not directly quantify fat loss.

Explanation:

Hirschsprung’s disease (Aganglionic megacolon):

It is due to congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in both myentric and meissner’s plexus in segment of distal colon due to failure of cranial to caudal migration of neural crest cells during development.

Causes:

  • Endothelial B receptor gene mutation.
  • Neural crest cell migration defect.
  • RET proto-oncogene mutation.

Symptoms:

  • Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life.
  • Abdominal distention.
  • Bilious vomiting.
  • Constipation.
  • Failure to thrive.

Clinical Features:

  • Lack of stool in the rectal vault on digital rectal examination.
  • Explosive release of gas and stool upon withdrawal of the examining finger (squirt sign).
  • Chronic constipation in older children.

 

Meconium ileus (Option A ruled out): Associated with cystic fibrosis. Usually involves obstruction in the distal ileum (not colon). X-ray: "Soap-bubble" appearance. NOT typically associated with a narrowed distal colon

Increased enteric ganglion cells (Option B ruled out): This would enhance motility, not cause obstruction. In Hirschsprung, the issue is lack of ganglion cells.

Intestinal atresia (Option   C ruled out): Usually presents with double bubble or triple bubble sign on X-ray, depending on location (duodenal, jejunal, etc.). Often has polyhydramnios in utero. Not typically associated with transition zone in colon

questions.stem: A 35 y/o patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals a dendritic ulcer on the cornea. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35 y/o patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals a dendritic ulcer on the cornea. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.solution: 50cb871692777180ce7d18e840">acyclovir and cycloplegics Explanation: The patient presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in the right eye, along with a dendritic ulcer on the cornea. This clinical picture is classic for Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK), an infection of the cornea caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). Treatment of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis: Topical Therapy: Antivirals: Acyclovir 3% ointment: 5 times daily. Other Topical Medications: Antibiotics: Prevent secondary bacterial infections, especially with epithelial defects. Cycloplegics: (e.g., Homatropine 1%) Relieve pain and photophobia by paralyzing ciliary muscles and dilating the pupil. Topical steroids and antibiotics (Option A): Topical steroids are contraindicated in the treatment of active epithelial HSV keratitis, as they can suppress the immune response and worsen the viral infection, potentially leading to complications like corneal perforation. Antibiotics are not needed unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not indicated here. Oral acyclovir and lubricants (Option B): While oral acyclovir is used in more severe or recurrent cases of HSV keratitis, topical acyclovir is preferred as the initial treatment. Lubricants can be supportive but are not the primary treatment. Oral steroids and topical antibiotics (Option D): Oral steroids are contraindicated in HSV keratitis, similar to topical steroids, as they can exacerbate the infection. Topical antibiotics are unnecessary unless there's evidence of bacterial superinfection. @Neet_pg_bot

Treatment of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis:

Topical Therapy: 

  • Antivirals:
    • Acyclovir 3% ointment: 5 times daily.
  • Other Topical Medications:
    • Antibiotics: Prevent secondary bacterial infections, especially with epithelial defects.
    • Cycloplegics: (e.g., Homatropine 1%) Relieve pain and photophobia by paralyzing ciliary muscles and dilating the pupil.

Topical steroids and antibiotics (Option A):

  • Antibiotics are not needed unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not indicated here.

Oral acyclovir and lubricants (Option B):

  • While oral acyclovir is used in more severe or recurrent cases of HSV keratitis, topical acyclovir is preferred as the initial treatment.
  • Lubricants can be supportive but are not the primary treatment.

Oral steroids and topical antibiotics (Option D):

  • Oral steroids are contraindicated in HSV keratitis, similar to topical steroids, as they can exacerbate the infection.
  • Topical antibiotics are unnecessary unless there's evidence of bacterial superinfection.

questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman presents with severe pain in her left hip and is unable to bear weight on the affected leg after slipping and falling at home. An X-ray reveals a fracture of the femoral neck. Using the Garden classification system for femoral neck fractures, what is the likely grade of this fracture?
questions.solution: Femoral Neck Fractures Intracapsular Fractures (90%) These fractures occur within the joint capsule and affect the neck of the femur, which is enclosed by the hip joint's synovial membrane. Extracapsular Fractures (10%) These fractures occur outside the joint capsule, typically affecting areas below the neck of the femur, such as the trochanteric and subtrochanteric regions. Anatomical Classification of Intracapsular Fractures This classification focuses on the specific location within the femoral neck where the fracture occurs. It differentiates between fractures just below the femoral head and those at the base of the neck. Type Description Prognosis/Complications Subcapital Fracture just below the femoral head. Most common; high risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion. Transcervical Fracture through the midportion of the femoral neck. Intermediate risk of complications. Basicervical Fracture at the base of the femoral neck. Lower risk of avascular necrosis but transitions to extracapsular fractures. Garden’s Classification Garden’s classification is widely used to assess the completeness and displacement of femoral neck fractures. It also uses the trabecular alignment in radiographs to estimate the severity of the fracture. Grade Fracture Details Trabecular Alignment Prognosis Grade I Incomplete, valgus-impacted fracture. Normal trabecular alignment. Best prognosis. Grade II Complete, but without displacement. Normal trabecular alignment. Good prognosis with fixation. Grade III Complete with partial displacement. Misalignment between head and acetabulum. Increased risk of nonunion. Grade IV Complete with full displacement. Trabecular pattern parallel but displaced. Worst prognosis. High risk of avascular necrosis. @Neet_pg_bot

These fractures occur within the joint capsule and affect the neck of the femur, which is enclosed by the hip joint's synovial membrane.

Extracapsular Fractures (10%)

  • Screening conducted during routine healthcare visits for other reasons

Positive Eugenics

The goal is to increase the prevalence of desirable traits in the population over generations.

This can be encouraged through various means such as:

  • Financial and political stimuli

  • Targeted demographic analyses

  • In vitro fertilisation

  • Egg transplants

  • Gene cloning

 

Negative Eugenics

The objective is to reduce the frequency of hereditary disease and disability in the community.

This could involve measures such as:

  • Abortions

  • Sterilizations

  • Other methods of family planning

 

Euthenics (Option A) focuses on improving human health and well-being by enhancing environmental and living conditions rather than altering genetic traits.

questions.solution: trong> The given clinical condition is diagnosed as Acne vulgaris, a chronic inflammatory skin condition associated with increased sebum production and the accumulation of dead skin cells within the follicles. Comedones are clogged hair follicles (pores) that contain a mixture of oil (sebum) and dead skin cells. They are the hallmark lesions of acne vulgaris. They are non-inflammatory lesions and are of two types: Open comedones (blackheads): These are follicles with a wider opening to the skin's surface and are not covered by the epidermis. When exposed to air, the keratin plug becomes oxidized and appears black. Closed comedones (whiteheads): These are follicles with a narrower opening to the skin's surface and are covered by the epidermis. The accumulation of sebum and dead skin cells creates a white or flesh-coloured bump beneath the skin's surface. It primarily affects individuals over the age of 40 and is also seen in adolescents (Option A): Acne vulgaris is typically seen in puberty and adolescence, not above the age of 40 years. It is not influenced by hormonal factors (Option B): Hormonal fluctuations, particularly increased levels of androgens (such as testosterone), can stimulate sebaceous gland activity, leading to increased sebum production. They are often associated with hormonal conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH). Genetic predisposition is not a contributing factor (Option D) : Genetic factors influence various aspects of acne development, including sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, and inflammatory responses. Thus, Genetic predisposition is a contributing factor to the development of acne vulgaris. @Neet_pg_bot

Death in Hanging

The usual period for death is 3–5 minutes and this can extend to 5–8 minutes of suspension leading to death.

  1. Immediate Death:
    • Occurs if cervical vertebrae are fractured.

Causes of Death from Hanging

  2. Venous Congestion: If the ligature is broad and soft, it can block the jugular veins, halting cerebral circulation. (Option C ruled out)

  4. Cerebral Anemia: Occurs when a thin cord is used as a ligature, reducing blood flow to the brain.
  5. Reflex Vagal Inhibition: This can result in sudden cardiac arrest. (Option D ruled out)
  6. Fracture/Dislocation of Cervical Vertebrae: Commonly seen in judicial hangings.

 

Delayed Deaths

Rarely, delayed deaths may result from:

  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Edema of the lungs or larynx
  • Infections

questions.solution: Male gender is not a risk factor for developing schizophrenia as it has equal prevalence in both sexes. Schizophrenia demographics: Equal prevalence in men and women. Men tend to have an earlier onset (ages 10-25) than women (ages 25-35). Men often experience more negative symptoms; women generally have better social functioning and outcomes. Late-onset schizophrenia occurs after age 45 (3-10% of women). 90% of treated patients are aged 15-55. Urban upbringing (Option C) : Risk is higher for those raised in cities. Cannabis use : Associated with increased risk of schizophrenia, particularly in heavy users (up to 40% increase ). questions.stem: While flowing through which of the following segments does the filtrate become progressively hypertonic compared to plasma?
questions.stemHtml: While flowing through which of the following segments does the filtrate become progressively hypertonic compared to plasma?
questions.solution: ustomMeta" data-dictid="32562f5afa1692777193c891837db9">nephron where the filtrate becomes progressively hypertonic compared to plasma is the Descending limb of the loop of Henle (Segment B). Descending limb of Loop of Henle: In the descending limb, the permeability to water allows for the passive reabsorption of water into the hypertonic medullary interstitium. This segment is impermeable to solutes such as sodium and chloride but permeable to water. As the filtrate descends into the medulla, where the interstitial osmolality is very high (up to 1200-1400 mOsm/kg), water moves out of the descending limb due to osmosis. This results in the filtrate becoming more concentrated (hypertonic) compared to plasma as it progresses through the descending limb. Thick Ascending limb of LOH (Segment C)(Option C) The ascending limb actively transports sodium, potassium, and chloride ions out of the filtrate into the interstitium, making the filtrate progressively hypotonic as ions are reabsorbed without water. Early Distal convoluted tubule (Segment D)(Option A) The early distal tubule has properties similar to those of the thick ascending loop of Henle, so further dilution of the tubular fluid occurs as solutes are reabsorbed while water remains in the tubule. Glomerulus (Segment A)(Option B) It’s a filtration process. No active transport or reabsorption occurs in the glomerulus itself that would change the osmolality of the filtrate. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ustomMeta" data-dictid="32562f5afa1692777193c891837db9">nephron where the filtrate becomes progressively hypertonic compared to plasma is the Descending limb of the loop of Henle (Segment B).

 

Descending limb of Loop of Henle:

  • In the descending limb, the permeability to water allows for the passive reabsorption of water into the hypertonic medullary interstitium.
  • This segment is impermeable to solutes such as sodium and chloride but permeable to water.
  • As the filtrate descends into the medulla, where the interstitial osmolality is very high (up to 1200-1400 mOsm/kg), water moves out of the descending limb due to osmosis.
  • This results in the filtrate becoming more concentrated (hypertonic) compared to plasma as it progresses through the descending limb.

Thick Ascending limb of LOH (Segment C)(Option C)

The ascending limb actively transports sodium, potassium, and chloride ions out of the filtrate into the interstitium, making the filtrate progressively hypotonic as ions are reabsorbed without water.

Early Distal convoluted tubule (Segment D)(Option A)

The early distal tubule has properties similar to those of the thick ascending loop of Henle, so further dilution of the tubular fluid occurs as solutes are reabsorbed while water remains in the tubule.

Glomerulus (Segment A)(Option B)

It’s a filtration process. No active transport or reabsorption occurs in the glomerulus itself that would change the osmolality of the filtrate.

Explanation:

The management of pressure sores depends on the stage and severity of the wound.

For a stage III pressure sore, conservative management is typically the initial approach, with surgery reserved for more advanced cases or when conservative measures fail.

 

Conservative management includes:

1. Pressure relief: Repositioning the patient every 2-3 hours

2. Wound care: Cleaning and dressing the wound

3. Nutritional support: Ensuring adequate protein and calorie intake

4. Hydrocolloid dressings: These maintain a moist environment, promote autolytic debridement, and protect the wound

 

Surgical management is considered for:

1. Stage III and IV pressure sores that fail to heal with conservative measures

2. Exposed bone, tendon, or joint

3. Undermining, tunneling, or sinus tract formation

 

Surgical options include:

Immediate surgical debridement (Option A) is incorrect as it's too aggressive for initial management.

Negative pressure wound therapy (Option C) is typically used after debridement and is not the first-line treatment.

Flap reconstruction (Option D) is a surgical option reserved for more advanced cases or when conservative measures fail.

Swinging flashlight test: The swinging flashlight test is used to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) , often seen with unilateral optic nerve lesions, even when visual acuity is normal. Procedure: Shine a bright flashlight on one pupil and observe its constriction. Quickly move the light to the contralateral pupil and observe the response. Repeat the process several times, alternating between the two eyes. Normal response: Both pupils constrict equally, and the pupil receiving the light remains tightly constricted. Abnormal response (RAPD): If there is a relative afferent pathway defect, the affected pupil will dilate when the light is moved from the normal eye to the abnormal eye. Significance: The presence of Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is an early indication of optic nerve disease, even when visual acuity appears normal. It aids in diagnosing eye conditions like glaucoma, retinal diseases, and neurological disorders affecting visual pathways. Tonometry (Option C) is a diagnostic test used in Glaucoma to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). The visual acuity test (Option D) measures the sharpness or clarity of a person's vision. questions.stem: What radiological feature distinguishes a sequestrum from living bone in a case of osteomyelitis?
questions.stemHtml: What radiological feature distinguishes a sequestrum from living bone in a case of osteomyelitis?
questions.solution: A sequestrum appears denser than the surrounding living bone on an X-ray because it is no longer involved in the normal bone remodelling or decalcification process. The lack of blood supply and ongoing inflammatory process preserve the mineral content, making it a bright, dense structure on imaging. Visually, they are pale in colour, with a smooth inner surface and a rough outer surface where surrounding tissue tries to erode it. Increased radiolucency (Option A): A sequestrum is denser and would appear brighter, not darker or more radiolucent, on an X-ray . Reduced density (Option B): Sequestra retain their density due to the lack of remodelling, so they appear denser, not less dense, than living bone. Fracture line (Option D): While a sequestrum can be separated from living bone, the appearance is typically characterized by increased density rather than a visible fracture line. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is characterized by the presence of compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands in the submucosa, and a muscular layer that transitions from skeletal to smooth muscle?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following structures is characterized by the presence of compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands in the submucosa, and a muscular layer that transitions from skeletal to smooth muscle?
questions.solution: "6a729a105a169277718788389dbeab">esophagus is lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and contains mucous glands (esophageal glands proper) in its submucosa for lubrication. Its muscular layer transitions from skeletal muscle (upper third) to smooth muscle (lower third), characteristic of the process of swallowing. Structure Description Esophagus Has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and adventitia. Lumen lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Submucosa - compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands, known as esophageal glands proper, which aid in lubrication. The upper third of the esophagus has predominantly skeletal muscle due to voluntary control during swallowing. In the middle third, there is a gradual transition to smooth muscle, and the lower third consists entirely of smooth muscle. Lacks a serous covering, except for a short section near its lower end. Stomach (Option B ruled out) The epithelium-forming glands are supported by Lamina Propria, a connective tissue. It has a peritoneum called serosa, which is missing from the oesophagus. Lined by Simple columnar epithelium and forms some gastric glands Mucosa contains gastric pits or gastric foveolae. The gastric glands contain: Surface mucous cells- Bicarbonate ions Mucous neck cells - mucus Parietal (Oxyntic) cells- HCL & Intrinsic Factor. Chief, peptic or zymogenic cells- Pepsin Neuroendocrine cells- Serotonin & Gastrin hormone. Small Intestine (Option C & D ruled out) Small intestine has columnar epithelium, which has villi, and microvilli leading to formation of brush border epithelium. The intestinal villi are lined by a simple columnar epithelium which is continuous with the crypts. Plicae circulares (Valves of Kerckring) are circular folds given by the mucosa and submucosa. Microvilli are finger-like projections to increase the surface area for absorption. Lymphoid clusters called Peyer’s patches are characteristically found in the lamina propria of the small intestine. Cells in the mucosa are: Enterocytes Paneth cells- defence Goblet cells- Mucin Neuroendocrine cells- hormones @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
"6a729a105a169277718788389dbeab">esophagus is lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and contains mucous glands (esophageal glands proper) in its submucosa for lubrication. Its muscular layer transitions from skeletal muscle (upper third) to smooth muscle (lower third), characteristic of the process of swallowing.

Structure

Description

Esophagus

 
  • Has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and adventitia.
  • Lumen lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
  • Submucosa- compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands, known as esophageal glands proper, which aid in lubrication.
  • The upper third of the esophagus has predominantly skeletal muscle due to voluntary control during swallowing.
  • In the middle third, there is a gradual transition to smooth muscle, and the lower third consists entirely of smooth muscle.
  • Lacks a serous covering, except for a short section near its lower end.

Stomach (Option B ruled out)
  • The epithelium-forming glands are supported by Lamina Propria, a connective tissue.
  • It has a peritoneum called serosa, which is missing from the oesophagus.
  • Lined by Simple columnar epithelium and forms some gastric glands
  • Mucosa contains gastric pits or gastric foveolae.
  • The gastric glands contain:
    • Surface mucous cells- Bicarbonate ions
    • Mucous neck cells- mucus
    • Parietal (Oxyntic) cells- HCL & Intrinsic Factor.
    • Chief, peptic or zymogenic cells- Pepsin
    • Neuroendocrine cells- Serotonin & Gastrin hormone.

Small Intestine (Option C & D ruled out)

 
  • Small intestine has columnar epithelium, which has villi, and microvilli leading to formation of brush border epithelium.
  • The intestinal villi are lined by a simple columnar epithelium which is continuous with the crypts.
  • Plicae circulares (Valves of Kerckring) are circular folds given by the mucosa and submucosa.
  • Microvilli are finger-like projections to increase the surface area for absorption.
  • Lymphoid clusters called Peyer’s patches are characteristically found in the lamina propria of the small intestine.
  • Cells in the mucosa are:
    • Enterocytes
    • Paneth cells- defence
    • Goblet cells- Mucin
    • Neuroendocrine cells- hormones

cularly in unvaccinated individuals, treatment requires thorough wound cleaning, a full series of rabies vaccinations, and Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) around the wound to provide immediate passive immunity.

Categories of dog bite and management:

Category

Exposure Type

Management

Category I

  • Touching or feeding animals

  • Licking of intact skin

  • Ensure proper hygiene

  • No treatment required

Category II

  • Nibbling on uncovered skin

  • Minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding

  • Immediate wound washing with soap and water

Category III

  • Licks on broken skin

  • Exposure to mucous membranes (mouth, eyes, nose)

    • Human rabies Immunoglobulin or HRIG
      • Preferred (free from the danger of sensitisation, HIV and hepatitis viruses)

questions.answerText: Excessive use of vitamin D preparations and phosphate binders
questions.solution: >Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity. The main cause is over-suppression of PTH , often iatrogenic. This occurs with: High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity.

  • The main cause is over-suppression of PTH, often iatrogenic.

  • This occurs with:

    • High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion

    • Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH

  • Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase.

questions.solution: elves. Explanation: Cleft palate occurs when the palatal shelves fail to elevate and fuse properly during embryonic development, typically between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation. This results in a gap in the palate, allowing communication between the oral and nasal cavities, as evidenced by milk coming through the nasal passages during feeding. Cleft palate: Defective fusion of the various components of the palate gives rise to clefts in the palate. Complete cleft palate: Bilateral complete cleft (A): Failure of fusion of both palatine processes of maxilla with premaxilla. A y-shaped cleft will be present between primary and secondary palate and between the two halves of secondary palate. It presents as a bilateral cleft of the upper lip also. Unilateral complete cleft (B): Nonfusion of one side palatine process of maxilla with premaxilla. It presents as a unilateral cleft of the upper lip. Incomplete cleft palate: Cleft of hard and soft palate( C): Cleft limited to hard palate. Cleft of soft palate (D): Cleft limited to hard palate. Bifid uvula (E): Cleft limited to uvula. Fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes (Option A): This contributes to formation of the upper lip and primary palate . Its failure leads to cleft lip , not cleft palate. Formation of the lateral palatine processes (Option B): While formation is important, fusion failure (not formation) is responsible for the defect in this case. Formation of the primary palate (Option D): The primary palate forms the region anterior to the incisive foramen; its failure causes anterior clefting , not posterior palatal clefts. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

 

  • Cleft palate occurs when the palatal shelves fail to elevate and fuse properly during embryonic development, typically between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation.
  • This results in a gap in the palate, allowing communication between the oral and nasal cavities, as evidenced by milk coming through the nasal passages during feeding.

Cleft palate:

Defective fusion of the various components of the palate gives rise to clefts in the palate.

 

Complete cleft palate:

  • Bilateral complete cleft (A): Failure of fusion of both palatine processes of maxilla with premaxilla. A y-shaped cleft will be present between primary and secondary palate and between the two halves of secondary palate. It presents as a bilateral cleft of the upper lip also.
  • Unilateral complete cleft (B): Nonfusion of one side palatine process of maxilla with premaxilla. It presents as a unilateral cleft of the upper lip.

 

Incomplete cleft palate:

  • Cleft of hard and soft palate( C): Cleft limited to hard palate.
  • Cleft of soft palate (D): Cleft limited to hard palate.
  • Bifid uvula (E): Cleft limited to uvula.

 

Fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes (Option A): This contributes to formation of the upper lip and primary palate. Its failure leads to cleft lip, not cleft palate.

Formation of the lateral palatine processes (Option B): While formation is important, fusion failure (not formation) is responsible for the defect in this case.

Formation of the primary palate (Option D): The primary palate forms the region anterior to the incisive foramen; its failure causes anterior clefting, not posterior palatal clefts.

cal scenario likely describes acute eczema that does not show lichenification, which is a feature of chronic eczema.

 

Eczema or atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic, inflammatory condition of the skin. The pattern of the rash varies with age

  • Infantile phase (<2 years): The lesions are present on the face and extensor aspect of the knees and elbows consisting of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules may become exudative and crusted.

 

  • Childhood phase (2 years to puberty): Presents as erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification involving the elbow and knee flexures.
  • Adult phase: Similar to the childhood phase with more localized and lichenified lesions.

 

Based on the duration of complaints, eczema may be acute, subacute, or chronic.

Acute eczema presents with itching and dryness of the skin. Examination findings include signs of inflammation - erythema, oedema, vesicles, oozing, and crusting.

 

 

Chronic eczema results from long-term untreated or inadequately treated eczema. Exam findings include lichenification, increased skin markings, hyperpigmentation, and thickening of the skin as shown below.


Subacute eczema lies in between acute and chronic eczema - erythema and scaling may be seen.
