questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer : Option B- Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency 

  • The scenario describes a child with severe fatigue, vomiting, nonketotic hypoglycemia, and fatty liver, alongside a maternal history of acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP).
  • These features are characteristic of Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency.
    • This condition affects fatty acid oxidation and can manifest in both the child and mother, particularly with AFLP during pregnancy.
  • Other deficiencies listed do not specifically present with this combination of symptoms and maternal history.

 

FATTY ACID OXIDATION DEFECTS

CONGENITAL DEFECTS

ACQUIRED DEFECTS

1. CPT-I Deficiency:

  • Site: Liver
  • Pathophysiology: Leading to decreased fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, which can result in hypoglycemia (Option A ruled out)
 

2. CPT-II Deficiency:

  • Site: Primarily affecting skeletal muscle and potentially the liver in severe cases
 

3. Defects in β-oxidation Enzymes: 2 types:

 
  • Long and Short-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency: Can cause nonketotic hypoglycemia, coma, and fatty liver. May also contribute to acute fatty liver during pregnancy
 
  • 3-Ketoacyl-CoA Thiolase and HMG-CoA Lyase Deficiency: These deficiencies not only disrupt fatty acid oxidation but also affect the breakdown of leucine, a ketogenic amino acid.

1. Carnitine Deficiency:

  • Common in preterm babies
  • Cause:
    • Inadequate biosynthesis or renal leakage.
    • Hemolysis
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Impaired fatty acid oxidation→hypoglycemia & Lipid accumulation→muscular weakness (Option D ruled out)
 

2. Jamaican Vomiting Sickness:

 
  • Cause: Consuming unripe ackee fruit containing the toxin hypoglycin,
  • Pathophysiology: This condition inhibits medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, leading to hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out)

CLINICAL FEATURES
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Nonketotic Hypoglycemia
  • Lipid Accumulation
  • Dicarboxylic Aciduria
    • Marked by the excretion of C6—C10 ω-dicarboxylic acids and non-ketotic hypoglycemia
    • It arises from a lack of mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
  • Muscular Weakness due to the buildup of lipids in muscles
  • Coma
  • Fatty Liver
  • Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy: Due to Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency indicating a potential role of hormonal changes influencing enzyme activity.
  • Neurological Symptoms: Defects impacting fatty acid oxidation, especially those also affecting the breakdown of leucine.

 

Differential Diagnosis:

  1. DKA (Benedict+, Rothera+): This would present with high blood glucose and elevated ketone bodies, which is not the case here.
  2. Starvation ketosis (Benedict-, Rothera+): This can also cause non-ketotic hypoglycemia, but without the fatty liver findings.
  3. Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): This amino acid disorder can impact fatty acid oxidation and cause hypoglycemia, but would likely present with a different pattern of symptoms.
  4. Type 1 Glycogen Storage Disease: This can also lead to fasting hypoglycemia, but would not typically involve fatty liver changes

The above clinical case is suggestive of chemical injury. Irrigation with water or saline is the priority to dilute and remove the chemical, minimizing damage.

Management of Chemical Injury

  • Immediate irrigation: Copious water/saline for 20–30 min or until pH normal; double eversion of lids.
  • Debridement: Removal of dead conjunctiva/corneal epithelium with cotton swab (Option A).
  • Antibiotics: To prevent secondary infection (Option A).

  • Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): 10% eye drops 2-hourly to promote collagen synthesis.
  • Collagenase inhibitors: Citrate 10% drops, tetracycline, acetylcysteine 10%.
  • Early surgical options: Tenon advancement, limbal cell transplant, amniotic membrane graft.

Complications: Secondary glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency, pseudopterygium, corneal opacity

questions.answerText: Support of spermatogenesis through FSH-mediated stimulation
questions.solution: : The most plausible explanation for the observed hormonal imbalances and clinical features is a compromised ability of Sertoli cells to respond to FSH stimulation , leading to both impaired spermatogenesis and, consequently, low testosterone levels. The reduced negative feedback from inhibin due to impaired Sertoli cell function further contributes to the elevated FSH levels. Hormones of Spermatogenesis: Follicular stimulating hormone: FSH is essential for the initial development of spermatogonia cells. Main targets of FSH action include: Proliferation of Sertoli cell Proliferation of Spermatogonia up to primary spermatocyte stage Support the process of meiosis. Testosterone: Testosterone is particularly required for the terminal stages of spermatogenesis Main targets of testosterone action include: Spermiogenesis (spermatid to mature sperm) Spermiation (release of sperm) Meiosis (suppression of testosterone leads to block in meiosis) Estrogen: Main targets of Estrogen include: Fluid resorption and concentration of sperm Acrosome biogenesis of sperm Growth hormone: Growth hormone specifically promotes early division of the spermatogonia Option A) Secretion of testosterone in response to LH stimulation is a function of Leydig cell Option B) Production of inhibin leading to increased FSH levels simply does not explain the low testosterone levels seen in this patient Option C) While testosterone does play a role in spermatogenesis, its production is mainly stimulated by LH acting on Leydig cells. @Neet_pg_bot

The most plausible explanation for the observed hormonal imbalances and clinical features is a compromised ability of Sertoli cells to respond to FSH stimulation, leading to both impaired spermatogenesis and, consequently, low testosterone levels. The reduced negative feedback from inhibin due to impaired Sertoli cell function further contributes to the elevated FSH levels.

 

Hormones of Spermatogenesis:

Follicular stimulating hormone:

  • FSH is essential for the initial development of spermatogonia cells.
  • Main targets of FSH action include:
    • Proliferation of Sertoli cell
    • Proliferation of Spermatogonia up to primary spermatocyte stage
    • Support the process of meiosis.

Testosterone:

  • Testosterone is particularly required for the terminal stages of spermatogenesis
  • Main targets of testosterone action include:
    • Spermiogenesis (spermatid to mature sperm)
    • Spermiation (release of sperm)
    • Meiosis (suppression of testosterone leads to block in meiosis)

Estrogen:

  • Main targets of Estrogen include:
    • Fluid resorption and concentration of sperm
    • Acrosome biogenesis of sperm

Growth hormone:

  • Growth hormone specifically promotes early division of the spermatogonia

 

Option A) Secretion of testosterone in response to LH stimulation is a function of Leydig cell

Option B) Production of inhibin leading to increased FSH levels simply does not explain the low testosterone levels seen in this patient

Option C) While testosterone does play a role in spermatogenesis, its production is mainly stimulated by LH acting on Leydig cells.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman with a 10-year history of poorly controlled hypertension visits your clinic for follow-up. Her blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg, despite being on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Her serum creatinine and potassium levels are within normal limits. Which calcium channel blockers would be the most appropriate addition to her long-term blood pressure control treatment regimen?
questions.solution: Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, and it would be an appropriate choice to achieve better blood pressure control in the long term. It can be used as an add-on therapy with other antihypertensive agents, and its once-daily dosing improves patient compliance. Mechanism of action of CCB (Dihydropyridines): It blocks the entry of calcium ions through the L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, causing vasodilation and a reduction in peripheral vascular resistance. Drug Use Rationale for Choice Nifedipine (Option A) Short-acting Primarily used for angina pectoris Not recommended for long-term hypertension management due to its short duration of action and potential for reflex tachycardia. Nicardipine (Option B) Short-acting Commonly used in the management of hypertensive emergencies and perioperative hypertension or severe hypertension in the intensive care unit. The short duration of action makes it less suitable for long-term hypertension management. Clevidipine (Option C) Ultra-short-acting Very short half-life makes it unsuitable for long-term hypertension management. Amlodipine (Option D) Long-acting. Recommended as a first-line or add-on therapy for the long-term management of hypertension Preferred choice due to its long duration of action (up to 24 hours), once-daily dosing, and effectiveness in lowering blood pressure with good tolerability. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: n alkaline urine. Appears as coffin-lid-shaped crystals and is always associated with urinary infections. Calcium Oxalate (Option A ruled out): Shapes include envelopes, spindles, ovals, octahedral, picket fences, or dumbbell-shaped. Often feature an "X" in the center. Calcium Phosphate: Colorless crystals that appear as plates, stars, stellate shapes, or clusters of needles or rosettes. Typically found in more alkaline urine. Cystine (Option D ruled out): Crystals are hexagonal in shape and resemble nearly perfect benzene rings under the microscope. Uric Acid (Option B ruled out): Crystals can be rhomboidal-shaped, rosettes, or plates. Found in acidic urine with a pH of 5.5 or lower. @Neet_pg_bot

pH: 7.52
pCO2: 38 mmHg
HCO3-: 32 mEq/L

The patient's primary issue is related to fluid and electrolyte imbalances due to vomiting, not a respiratory or oxygenation problem. Start acetazolamide (Option D): Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that can be used to correct metabolic alkalosis by increasing renal bicarbonate excretion. However, the immediate need is to address the underlying cause of the alkalosis, which in this case is due to chloride loss from vomiting. Normal saline is usually the initial treatment of choice. @Neet_pg_bot

O/E, the patient has distended neck veins with the following waveform with a blowing holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old male with a history of long-standing hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents with progressive fatigue & bilateral leg swelling. O/E, the patient has distended neck veins with the following waveform with a blowing holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ricuspid regurgitation, as the patient presents with jugular venous distension (prominent C-V waves, rapid Y descent) , ascites, and hepatomegaly. The characteristic finding is a blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, which increases with inspiration. Pulmonary hypertension (Option A) can cause right-sided heart failure, but it does not typically present with a holosystolic murmur or intensification of the murmur with inspiration. Instead, the primary finding is a loud P2 sound due to increased pressure in the pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary stenosis (Option C) presents with an ejection systolic murmur heard best over the pulmonic area, not a holosystolic murmur, and does not typically intensify with inspiration. Mitral regurgitation (Option D) causes a holosystolic murmur , which is best heard at the apex and radiates to the axilla. As it involves the left side of the heart, mitral regurgitation does not intensify with inspiration, and the jugular venous findings are not typical of left-sided heart disease. @Neet_pg_bot

ricuspid regurgitation, as the patient presents with jugular venous distension (prominent C-V waves, rapid Y descent), ascites, and hepatomegaly. The characteristic finding is a blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, which increases with inspiration.

Pulmonary hypertension (Option A) can cause right-sided heart failure, but it does not typically present with a holosystolic murmur or intensification of the murmur with inspiration. Instead, the primary finding is a loud P2 sound due to increased pressure in the pulmonary arteries.

Pulmonary stenosis (Option C) presents with an ejection systolic murmur heard best over the pulmonic area, not a holosystolic murmur, and does not typically intensify with inspiration.

Mitral regurgitation (Option D) causes a holosystolic murmur, which is best heard at the apex and radiates to the axilla. As it involves the left side of the heart, mitral regurgitation does not intensify with inspiration, and the jugular venous findings are not typical of left-sided heart disease.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following biochemical reactions is not regulated by allosteric regulation?
questions.solution: "af3ae60c0c16927771889b84ca41c0">glucose to glucose-6-phosphate. Unlike some other enzymes, glucokinase is primarily regulated by product inhibition (glucose-6-phosphate) rather than allosteric regulation. Allosteric regulation is a mechanism where an enzyme's activity is modified by the binding of an effector molecule at a site other than the active site, known as the allosteric site. Allosteric Site: A specific location on an enzyme distinct from the active site where effector molecules bind, inducing conformational changes that influence enzyme activity. Effectors: Molecules that bind to the allosteric site and modify enzyme activity. Conformational Changes : Binding of an effector to the allosteric site causes a conformational change in the enzyme, which can alter the enzyme's affinity for its substrate and modify the enzyme's catalytic efficiency.   • Allosteric Site: A specific location on an enzyme distinct from the active site where effector molecules bind, inducing conformational changes that influence enzyme activity.
  • Effectors: Molecules that bind to the allosteric site and modify enzyme activity.
  • Conformational Changes: Binding of an effector to the allosteric site causes a conformational change in the enzyme, which can alter the enzyme's affinity for its substrate and modify the enzyme's catalytic efficiency.

Which of the following pigments is most likely responsible for the brown discolouration of the liver observed in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 83-year-old man presents to his gastroenterologist with complaints of fatigue and discomfort in the upper abdomen. He has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes medications regularly. On physical examination, the liver edge is palpable below the right costal margin, indicating hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal mildly elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following pigments is most likely responsible for the brown discolouration of the liver observed in this patient?
questions.solution: upper abdominal discomfort, and physical examination reveals hepatomegaly; mildly elevated liver enzymes are noted on lab tests, and the brown discoloration of the liver is most likely due to the pigment Lipofuscin . Lipofuscin, also known as lipochrome or wear-and-tear pigment, is an insoluble pigment derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated lipids in intracellular membranes. It is a telltale sign of free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. It is responsible for the brown atrophy of the liver and heart, where lipofuscin accumulates in the hepatocytes and cardiac myocytes, respectively, due to oxidative damage and impaired cellular turnover, particularly with increasing age. It is also seen in senile atrophy (pigment of the old age). In histopathological examination, it appears as a yellow-brown, finely granular cytoplasmic pigment, often deposited in the perinuclear region. The special stain used for lipofuscin is Oil red O and Acid-fast / Ziehl–Neelsen stain. {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.solution: ictid="84294069061692777198bdff94a950">seroma formation Explanation: In this scenario, the accumulation of fluid beneath the graft is indicative of hematoma or seroma formation. This complication can prevent proper adherence of the graft to the wound bed, leading to graft failure if not addressed promptly. Hematomas are collections of blood, while seromas are accumulations of clear fluid. Both can occur when there is inadequate hemostasis or when there is excessive movement or pressure on the graft site post-operatively. Complications of Skin Grafting: Graft Failure (Option A ruled out) : This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement. It is not characterized by fluid accumulation beneath the graft. It can be prevented by ensuring good contact between the graft and the wound bed and avoiding movement or pressure on the graft. Infection (Option C ruled out) : Infection typically presents with redness, warmth, and pus rather than just fluid accumulation. Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections. Hematoma or Seroma Formation (Option B) : Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft. Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out) : If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory. Careful selection of graft thickness and meticulous placement can help achieve a better aesthetic outcome. @Neet_pg_bot

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome

Cause

Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT)

Inheritance

X-linked recessive

Variants
  • Classic Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: Undetectable HPRT levels.
  • Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome: Partial HPRT deficiency with variable neurological dysfunction.

Clinical Features
  • Self-injurious behaviour: Biting lips, fingers, tongue; begins with tooth eruption.
  • Cognitive impairment: Intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
  • Movement disorder: Starts with hypotonia, progresses to dystonia, choreoathetosis, oromandibular dystonia, and inspiratory stridor.

  • Hyperuricemia: Causes gout and kidney stones.
  • Neurological symptoms: Abnormalities in the dopamine system, reduced dopamine transporters.

Treatment
  • Allopurinol: Reduces uric acid levels and manages hyperuricemia
  • Symptom management: Controls movement disorders and self-injurious behaviours.

questions.solution: Melanin is a pigment produced by cells called melanocytes, and it plays a critical role in determining the colour of our skin, hair, and eyes. Tyrosinase catalyzes the first two steps in the conversion of the amino acid tyrosine to melanin . Tyrosine → L-Dopa → Dopaquinone Without enough functional tyrosinase, melanin production is reduced or completely absent, leading to the characteristic features of albinism. Phenylalanine hydroxylase (Option C) is an enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. A deficiency in this enzyme leads to phenylketonuria (PKU). S-adenosylmethionine (Option D) required for: Norepinephrine to Epinephrine: Enzyme: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT). Conversion of Homocysteine to Methionine: Enzyme: Methionine synthase, using methylcobalamin as a cofactor. Methylation of DNA: SAM donates methyl groups to cytosine residues, affecting gene expression. Synthesis of Creatine: SAM is involved in the methylation of guanidinoacetate to form creatine. Methylation of Neurotransmitters: SAM is also involved in the methylation of other neurotransmitters, including serotonin to melatonin. Lipid Metabolism: Involved in the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine from phosphatidylethanolamine. @Neet_pg_bot

Degrees of perineal tear

Description

First Degree (Option A)

Injury to perineal skin only.

Second Degree (Option B)

Injury to perineum involving perineal body (muscles) but not involving the anal sphincter.

Third Degree (Option C)

Injury to perineum, involving the anal sphincter complex (both external and internal):

Fourth degree (Option D)

Injury to perineum involving the anal sphincter complex (EAS and IAS) and anal epithelium.

This obstruction severely reduces venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities, leading to clinical manifestations such as: Variable degrees of swelling of head, neck and arms along with cyanosis. questions.solutionHtml:
iven scenario suggests superior vena cava syndrome (SVC), and a CT scan is the investigation choice for this condition.

 

Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome:

  • It occurs when the superior vena cava is obstructed, often due to bulky mediastinal lymph nodes or a right upper lobe tumour compressing or invading the vessel.
  • This obstruction severely reduces venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities, leading to clinical manifestations such as:
    • Variable degrees of swelling of head, neck and arms along with cyanosis.
    • Headache, conjunctival oedema, dizziness, and syncope can be seen
    • Some other features, such as nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, and tongue swelling, may also be seen.
    • Dyspnea, dysphagia, cough and hoarseness of voice can also be seen in case of compression of mediastinal structures.

  • Chest X-ray suggests a widening of superior mediastinum (Option A).
  • The investigation of choice is CT scan (Option D).
  • MRI (Option B) and ultrasound (Option C) are not the investigations of choice, though mediastinal mass can be seen and diagnosed.
  • Management of this syndrome depends on the cause.
  • In cases of tracheal obstruction, a tracheostomy might be done.

questions.solution: 199fc69bd7c56">Spinal cord Explanation: This clinical scenario is classic for Subacute Combined Degeneration due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, which affects both the dorsal columns (causing loss of vibration sense, positive Romberg sign) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (causing weakness and bilateral Babinski sign). The presence of absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar response suggests a mixed UMN and LMN picture seen in SACD as it involves both peripheral nerves and dorsal column. Note that neurological features can exist without hematological featuers. Incorrect options Tabes dorsalis also affects dorsal columns and can cause sensory ataxia, but there is no UMN involvement (Babinski sign would not be present). 199fc69bd7c56">Spinal cord

 

Explanation:

This clinical scenario is classic for Subacute Combined Degeneration  due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, which affects both the dorsal columns (causing loss of vibration sense, positive Romberg sign) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (causing weakness and bilateral Babinski sign). The presence of absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar response suggests a mixed UMN and LMN picture seen in SACD as it involves both peripheral nerves and dorsal column. 

Note that neurological features can exist without hematological featuers. 

Incorrect options 

Tabes dorsalis also affects dorsal columns and can cause sensory ataxia, but there is no UMN involvement (Babinski sign would not be present). 
Friedreich’s ataxia has onset in adolescence and has cardiomyopathy, and a family history, which are not mentioned.
Brown-Séquard syndrome presents with  ipsilateral motor and vibration loss with contralateral pain loss not a bilateral symmetrical presentation as seen here.

questions.stem: A 45 y/o male undergoes abdominal surgery and requires fluid replacement. The patient has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following fluids is most appropriate for maintenance during surgery to avoid the risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 y/o male undergoes abdominal surgery and requires fluid replacement. The patient has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following fluids is most appropriate for maintenance during surgery to avoid the risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.solution: 's Lactate is often preferred because it contains a buffer (lactate) that helps to mitigate the risk of acidosis. It is isotonic and provides electrolytes in a more balanced way, making it a suitable option for patients with CKD. Ringer's Lactate (Balanced Crystalloid) Usage : Maintenance fluid during surgery. Advantage : Prevents hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, unlike normal saline. Excretion : Rapid elimination due to suppression of ADH secretion, promoting diuresis. Buffer : Lactate metabolised to bicarbonate, maintaining or slightly increasing HCO3− levels, hence preventing acidosis. ½ NS (0.45% NaCl, Hypotonic Saline) Usage : Maintenance fluid in the postoperative period along with 4% dextrose. Risk : To minimize the risk of hyponatremia, excessive use of hypotonic solutions, particularly in the postoperative phase, is discouraged. 3% NS (3% NaCl, Hypertonic Saline) Usage : Treatment of symptomatic hyponatremia and cerebral oedema. Mechanism : Draws water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, aiding in plasma volume expansion. Caution : Careful electrolyte and osmolality monitoring is required to avoid complications like osmotic demyelination. There is also a potential to cause fluid overload and hypernatremia, not recommended as a maintenance fluid. (Option C) 0.9% Normal Saline (Option A) : It may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to its high chloride content. 5% Dextrose in Water (Option D) : This hypotonic solution is used primarily for free water replacement, not surgical maintenance. It is usually used perioperatively and must be avoided in the postoperative period as it can severely dilute plasma electrolytes and osmolality. Note: An isotonic solution in the postoperative period could lead to potential GI dysfunction, when administered in excess, due to increased mucosal edema. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
's Lactate is often preferred because it contains a buffer (lactate) that helps to mitigate the risk of acidosis.
  • It is isotonic and provides electrolytes in a more balanced way, making it a suitable option for patients with CKD.

    •  

    Ringer's Lactate (Balanced Crystalloid)

    • Usage: Maintenance fluid during surgery.
    • Advantage: Prevents hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, unlike normal saline.
    • Excretion:
      • Rapid elimination due to suppression of ADH secretion, promoting diuresis.

    • Buffer: Lactate metabolised to bicarbonate, maintaining or slightly increasing HCO3− levels, hence preventing acidosis.

     

    ½ NS (0.45% NaCl, Hypotonic Saline)

    • Usage: Maintenance fluid in the postoperative period along with 4% dextrose.
    • Risk: To minimize the risk of hyponatremia, excessive use of hypotonic solutions, particularly in the postoperative phase, is discouraged.

    3% NS (3% NaCl, Hypertonic Saline)

    • Usage: Treatment of symptomatic hyponatremia and cerebral oedema.
    • Mechanism: Draws water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, aiding in plasma volume expansion.
    • Caution: Careful electrolyte and osmolality monitoring is required to avoid complications like osmotic demyelination. There is also a potential to cause fluid overload and hypernatremia, not recommended as a maintenance fluid. (Option C)

    0.9% Normal Saline (Option A): It may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to its high chloride content.

    5% Dextrose in Water (Option D):

    • This hypotonic solution is used primarily for free water replacement, not surgical maintenance.
    • It is usually used perioperatively and must be avoided in the postoperative period as it can severely dilute plasma electrolytes and osmolality.

    Note: An isotonic solution in the postoperative period could lead to potential GI dysfunction, when administered in excess, due to increased mucosal edema.

rted on linagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor that requires no dosage adjustment for renal impairment in this patient with type-2 diabetes and end-stage kidney disease (eGFR = 30 mL/min/1.73 m2).

 

 

Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors:

MOA
  • Increase Incretin Levels: Prevents degradation of incretin hormones (GLP-1 and GIP)
  • Enhance Insulin Secretion from the pancreas in response to meals. (no risk of hypoglycemia)
  • Reduce Glucagon Secretion
  • Maintain neutral weight

Uses
  • Oral hypoglycemic drug (type-2 diabetes)

Drugs
  1. Linagliptin: Safe in renal failure
  2. Teneligliptin: Safe in renal failure
  3. Vildagliptin: Hepatotoxic
  4. Alogliptin
  5. Sitagliptin
  6. Saxagliptin: (Option B)
    1. Metabolised by CYP3A4, it has more drug interactions.
    2. Requires dose adjustment in renal impairment.
    3. Risk of congestive heart failure.

Side effects
  • Nausea and vomiting (most common)
  • Pancreatitis (lesser than GLP-1)
  • Risk of pancreatic and thyroid cancer (lesser than GLP-1)
  • Arthritis, Nasopharyngitis:
    • Increase interleukins and cytokines levels (similar structure to CD26)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions: Steven-Johnson syndrome, angioedema


 

Dapagliflozin (Option A), an SGLT-2 inhibitor, is not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus whose eGFR is less than 45 mL/min/1.73 m2.

 

Exenatide (Option C), a GLP-1 analogue, is avoided in patients with end-stage renal disease or ischemic renal failure due to hypovolemia.

questions.solution: se:collapse; width:624px"> Definition Postpartum thyroiditis is an inflammation of the thyroid gland that occurs after childbirth, typically within the first year postpartum Etiology Autoimmune Factors Genetic Predisposition Hormonal Changes Clinical manifestations It has 2 phases which has a clinical progression- Thyrotoxic phase ( 1-4 months) (Option A) Hypothyroid phase ( 4 to 8 months) (Option B) The hypothyroid phase either leads to euthyroid phase (Option C) or permanent hypothyroidism (Option D). Investigation Thyroid Function Tests : TSH: Elevated in the hypothyroid phase, suppressed in the hyperthyroid phase. Free T4: Elevated in the hyperthyroid phase, decreased in the hypothyroid phase. se:collapse; width:624px">

Definition

Postpartum thyroiditis is an inflammation of the thyroid gland that occurs after childbirth, typically within the first year postpartum

Etiology

  • Autoimmune Factors
  • Genetic Predisposition
  • Hormonal Changes

Clinical manifestations

It has 2 phases which has a clinical progression-

Thyrotoxic phase( 1-4 months) (Option A)

Hypothyroid phase( 4 to 8 months) (Option B)

The hypothyroid phase either leads to euthyroid phase (Option C) or permanent hypothyroidism (Option D).

Investigation

Thyroid Function Tests:

  • TSH: Elevated in the hypothyroid phase, suppressed in the hyperthyroid phase.
  • Free T4: Elevated in the hyperthyroid phase, decreased in the hypothyroid phase.
  • Free T3: May also be elevated in the hyperthyroid phase.

Thyroid Antibodies:

  • Anti-thyroid Peroxidase (Anti-TPO) Antibodies: Often elevated, indicating an autoimmune component.

Treatment:

  1. Hyperthyroid phase- Beta blockers
  2. Hypothyroid phase- Levothyroxine, (25 mcg to 75 mcg)

questions.stemHtml: An 80-year-old female patient came with complaints of gradual progressive diminution of vision for 2 years in both her eyes. She reports that over the last year, she noticed an improvement in her ability to read without glasses. The following finding is seen on slit lamp examination over the right eye and the left eye has similar opacity. Choose the most appropriate course of management for this patient.

options.label: A
options.text: Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses.

questions.solution: gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight” ), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice. Management: Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment. Cataract surgeries: ICCE (not preferred now) ECCE SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery) Phacoemulsification (most preferred) Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred. Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity. Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract. Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male patient presents with episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Which of the following mechanisms is associated with the pathogenesis of this condition?

options.label: C
options.text: Dilatation of the internal auditory artery

questions.solution: n of endolymph Explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Meniere’s disease, which is primarily associated with increased endolymph volume within the inner ear resulting from defective absorption/increased production of endolymph leading to increased endolymphatic pressure, which manifests as vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Etiopathogenesis of Meniere’s disease: Aetiology: Increased Endolymph Volume (Option A) Defective Absorption (Option B) Vasomotor Disturbances: Sympathetic overactivity causing spasms in the internal auditory artery (Option C) may disrupt cochlear or vestibular function, leading to vertigo and hearing loss. Allergy: Allergic reactions may cause the inner ear to produce excess endolymph. Many patients with Meniere’s disease have related allergies. Sodium and Water Retention: Excess fluid retention can exacerbate endolymphatic hydrops, so reducing salt intake is recommended. Hypothyroidism (Option D) : A small percentage of cases are linked to hypothyroidism and can improve with thyroid replacement therapy. Autoimmune and Viral Factors (Herpes family) Pathology: Meniere’s disease is characterised by distension of the endolymphatic system, particularly affecting the cochlear duct (scala media) and saccule, with possible involvement of the utricle and semicircular canals. The cochlear duct can expand, pushing the Reissner's membrane into the scala vestibuli, potentially leading to the rupture of this membrane and mixing of perilymph with endolymph causing the classic symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

The given scenario is suggestive of Meniere’s disease, which is primarily associated with increased endolymph volume within the inner ear resulting from defective absorption/increased production of endolymph leading to increased endolymphatic pressure, which manifests as vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.

 

Etiopathogenesis of Meniere’s disease:

Aetiology:

  • Increased Endolymph Volume (Option A)
  • Defective Absorption (Option B)
  • Vasomotor Disturbances: Sympathetic overactivity causing spasms in the internal auditory artery (Option C) may disrupt cochlear or vestibular function, leading to vertigo and hearing loss.
  • Allergy: Allergic reactions may cause the inner ear to produce excess endolymph. Many patients with Meniere’s disease have related allergies.
  • Sodium and Water Retention: Excess fluid retention can exacerbate endolymphatic hydrops, so reducing salt intake is recommended.
  • Hypothyroidism (Option D): A small percentage of cases are linked to hypothyroidism and can improve with thyroid replacement therapy.
  • Autoimmune and Viral Factors (Herpes family)

 

Pathology:

  • Meniere’s disease is characterised by distension of the endolymphatic system, particularly affecting the cochlear duct (scala media) and saccule, with possible involvement of the utricle and semicircular canals.
  • The cochlear duct can expand, pushing the Reissner's membrane into the scala vestibuli, potentially leading to the rupture of this membrane and mixing of perilymph with endolymph causing the classic symptoms.

questions.solutionHtml:
31621d">trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) or Turner syndrome (45, XO), are commonly associated with non-immune hydrops fetalis. These genetic conditions can disrupt normal fetal development, leading to cardiovascular abnormalities and fluid accumulation.

Causes of Non-Immune Hydrops Fetalis

Chromosomal abnormality (20%)
  • Trisomies (13, 18, 21)
  • Turner syndrome

Congenital cardiac lesions (15%)
  • Congenital heart block
  • Supraventricular tachycardia

Congenital abnormalities
  • Diaphragmatic hernia
  • Renal abnormality
  • Cystic hygroma.

Hematological
  • Beta-thalassemia
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Leukemia

Infections (14%)
  • Parvovirus
  • Rubella
  • Toxoplasma

Placental and Umbilical Cord Pathology
  • Twin-to-twin transfusion
  • Chorioangioma
  • Umbilical vein thrombosis

Maternal Diseases

  • Uncontrolled diabetes
  • Severe anemia
  • Thyrotoxicosis

 

Maternal Rh incompatibility (Option A) can lead to immune hydrops fetalis (not non-immune hydrops) in which maternal antibodies against fetal red blood cells cause hemolysis and subsequent fluid accumulation in the fetus.

Gestational diabetes (Option B) is not typically associated with non-immune hydrops fetalis. It primarily affects fetal growth and can lead to macrosomia (large fetus) and other metabolic issues.

Mild maternal hypertension (Option D) alone is unlikely to cause non-immune hydrops fetalis. Severe maternal hypertension (pre-eclampsia) with placental insufficiency can lead to fetal growth restriction and sometimes hydrops, but this is less common than other causes like chromosomal abnormalities.

questions.stem: A woman presents at 33 weeks of gestation and the umbilical artery doppler imaging shows the following finding. What is the next step of management?
questions.stemHtml: A woman presents at 33 weeks of gestation and the umbilical artery doppler imaging shows the following finding. What is the next step of management?

options.label: D
options.text: Terminate the pregnancy at 34 weeks of gestation

questions.solution: he umbilical artery doppler depicts reversal of end diastolic flow as waves appearing below baseline which is seen in intrauterine growth restriction. As the period of gestation has exceeded 32 weeks , the pregnancy can be terminated. In case of absent end diastolic flow, the waves just touch the baseline but dont appear below it. This suggest fetal compromise, hence the pregnancy is terminated by C Section if >34 weeks. Cardiovascular conditions contraindicated to pregnancy:

questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old child from a region with known iodine deficiency presents to the clinic with symptoms including developmental delay, short stature, and coarse facial features. The child’s parents report a high prevalence of goiter in their community. To prevent similar cases in the future, which of the following preventive measures is the most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Prescribing high-dose thyroid hormone replacement therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Recommending the use of iodinated salt or iodized oil

options.label: C
options.text: Advising on a diet high in vegetables and fruits

options.label: D
options.text: Performing regular thyroid function tests for all community members

questions.answerText: Recommending the use of iodinated salt or iodized oil
questions.solution: y disorders, including endemic cretinism, are best prevented through the use of iodinated salt or iodized oil. This approach addresses the root cause of iodine deficiency and is effective in preventing the associated disorders. Endemic Cretinism: Endemic cretinism is associated with endemic goiter and severe iodine deficiency. It manifests in two main forms: neurological cretinism and myxedematous cretinism A 14-year-old boy with a large nodular goiter - in an area of severe iodine-deficiency disorders in northern Morocco. Types of Endemic Cretinism: Neurological Cretinism : Characterized by deaf-mutism, squint, proximal spasticity and rigidity, and severe intellectual disability. Myxedematous Cretinism : Characterized by less severe intellectual impairment, severe short stature, coarse facial features, and myxedema. Prevention and Control: Prevention : Iodine deficiency disorders are best prevented through iodinated salt or iodized oil, as treatment is largely ineffective. Treatment : While signs of hypothyroidism may improve, neuromotor and intellectual deficiencies are irreversible. Surgical removal of large goiters is reserved for airway obstruction or cosmetic reasons. National Goiter Control Program (India): Launched in 1962 to control iodine deficiency disorders through salt iodination. Recommended daily iodine intake: 40-120 µg for children under 10 years. 150 µg for older children and adults. Additional 25-50 µg during pregnancy and lactation. Prescribing high-dose thyroid hormone replacement therapy (Option A): This option is not a preventive measure. While thyroid hormone replacement therapy can treat hypothyroidism and its symptoms, it does not prevent iodine deficiency or its associated disorders, such as endemic cretinism. Advising on a diet high in vegetables and fruits (Option C): While a healthy diet is beneficial for overall health, vegetables and fruits alone do not provide sufficient iodine to prevent iodine deficiency disorders. Performing regular thyroid function tests for all community members (Option D) focuses on monitoring rather than prevention. Regular thyroid function tests are useful for diagnosing thyroid disorders but do not prevent iodine deficiency. @Neet_pg_bot

Advising on a diet high in vegetables and fruits (Option C): While a healthy diet is beneficial for overall health, vegetables and fruits alone do not provide sufficient iodine to prevent iodine deficiency disorders.

 

Performing regular thyroid function tests for all community members (Option D) focuses on monitoring rather than prevention. Regular thyroid function tests are useful for diagnosing thyroid disorders but do not prevent iodine deficiency.

iopathogenesis mechanisms for primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) are given in the table below:

Risk Factors

Mechanisms

Demographic factors:

  • Age: 6th and 7th decades of life
  • Gender: Female to male ratio 1:3
  • Ethnicity: More common in Asians

1. Pupillary block (70% of cases): (Option A ruled out)

  • Most common mechanism (70% of cases)
  • Increased contact between iris and lens
  • Precipitating factors:
    • Physiological mydriasis (e.g., dim illumination, emotional stress)
    • Pharmacological mydriasis (e.g., tropicamide, cyclopentolate)
  • Results in relative pupil block

Anatomical factors:

  • Hypermetropic eyes
  • Shallow anterior chamber
  • Short axial length
  • Thick, anteriorly positioned lens
  • Small corneal diameter
  • Plateau iris configuration

2. Plateau iris configuration:

  • Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes
  • More common in younger patients (Option C ruled out)
  • Can persist after iridotomy
  • Associated with angle closure glaucoma without pupillary block

Other factors:

  • Family history
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Certain medications (e.g., topiramate)

3. Phacomorphic mechanism: (Option B ruled out)

  • Swollen lens contributes to angle closure
  • Can cause pupillary block or push peripheral iris forward
  • Can occur in acute or chronic forms
  • Associated with intumescent or other lens morphological abnormalities

questions.solution: Explanation: The POCSO Act is gender-neutral, and it protects all children, not just female children, under the age of 18 from sexual abuse. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act Enacted in 2012, it is law in India designed to protect children under the age of 18 from sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and pornography. Key Features of the POCSO Act: Gender-neutral law (Option A) It covers penetrative and non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, and use of children for pornography Burden of proof is on the accused, unlike many other criminal laws where the burden is on the prosecution Mandatory reporting by adults and failure to do so can be punishable Special courts for the trial of offenses to ensure a child-friendly environment Identity of the victim is to be protected, and the proceedings are to be conducted in camera to prevent exposure Recent Changes and Developments in the POCSO Act: 2019 Amendment (Option C ruled out) Stricter Punishments: Death penalty for aggravated sexual assault against children The minimum punishment for penetrative sexual assault increased to 10 years, and for aggravated penetrative sexual assault increased to 20 years, with the possibility of life imprisonment or death in extreme cases. Fast-track Courts to ensure swift disposal of POCSO cases, given the backlog of pending cases. (Option D ruled out) Clarifications on ‘Touch’ and Sexual Intent: The intent behind physical contact is crucial in determining whether it qualifies as an offense under POCSO. Digital Crimes Against Children: (Option B ruled out) Provisions related to the use of children for pornographic and online exploitation purposes have been emphasized with stricter penalties. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation: The POCSO Act is gender-neutral, and it protects all children, not just female children, under the age of 18 from sexual abuse.

 

Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act

Enacted in 2012, it is law in India designed to protect children under the age of 18 from sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and pornography.

 

Key Features of the POCSO Act:

  • Gender-neutral law (Option A)
  • It covers penetrative and non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, and use of children for pornography
  • Burden of proof is on the accused, unlike many other criminal laws where the burden is on the prosecution
  • Mandatory reporting by adults and failure to do so can be punishable
  • Special courts for the trial of offenses to ensure a child-friendly environment
  • Identity of the victim is to be protected, and the proceedings are to be conducted in camera to prevent exposure

 

Recent Changes and Developments in the POCSO Act:

  • 2019 Amendment (Option C ruled out)
    • Stricter Punishments: Death penalty for aggravated sexual assault against children
    • The minimum punishment for penetrative sexual assault increased to 10 years, and for aggravated penetrative sexual assault increased to 20 years, with the possibility of life imprisonment or death in extreme cases.
  • Fast-track Courts to ensure swift disposal of POCSO cases, given the backlog of pending cases. (Option D ruled out)
  • Clarifications on ‘Touch’ and Sexual Intent:
    • The intent behind physical contact is crucial in determining whether it qualifies as an offense under POCSO.
  • Digital Crimes Against Children: (Option B ruled out)
    • Provisions related to the use of children for pornographic and online exploitation purposes have been emphasized with stricter penalties.

questions.solution: Pneumonia is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in acute measles and is the most likely immediate complication in this case, especially in an unvaccinated child. Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. It primarily affects children and is transmitted through respiratory droplets or small-particle aerosols . questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency room after a motor vehicle accident. He displays significant behavioral changes including placing non-food objects in his mouth, increased sexual advances towards staff, and appears to have no fear when approached by the medical team. questions.solution: e581692777181a270cc1ca1">Amygdala Explanation: The case presents a patient with classic symptoms of Klüver-Bucy syndrome , including a lack of fear, oral tendencies, and hypersexuality. It is a rare behavioral disorder that can occur after damage to the anterior temporal lobes, including the amygdalae , which are almond-shaped groups of nuclei located deep within the temporal lobes. The amygdala is responsible for processing emotions, especially fear and reward. The symptoms of Klüver-Bucy syndrome are varied but can include the following: Lack of Fear : Individuals may show no fear of objects or situations that would normally elicit a fear response. Excessive Curiosity : They may display an intense interest in exploring their surroundings, often in a non-directed and inappropriate manner. Memory Impairment : Short-term memory is often significantly affected, leading to an inability to recall recent events. Oral Tendencies : A tendency to put objects in their mouth, even those that are not edible. Hypersexuality : An increased and often inappropriate sexual drive. Cerebellum (Option A): Responsible for motor coordination and balance . Damage → ataxia , dysmetria, intention tremor. Does not cause behavioral symptoms like hypersexuality or hyperorality. Hippocampus (Option C): Critical for forming new memories . Damage → anterograde amnesia . Does not cause hypersexuality or placidity . Parietal lobe (Option D): Involved in spatial awareness , sensory integration , and body awareness . Damage can cause hemineglect , apraxia , or Gerstmann syndrome . Behavioral disinhibition is not typical . @Neet_pg_bot

e581692777181a270cc1ca1">Amygdala

 

Explanation:

The case presents a patient with classic symptoms of Klüver-Bucy syndrome, including a lack of fear, oral tendencies, and hypersexuality.

  • It is a rare behavioral disorder that can occur after damage to the anterior temporal lobes, including the amygdalae, which are almond-shaped groups of nuclei located deep within the temporal lobes.
  • The amygdala is responsible for processing emotions, especially fear and reward.

The symptoms of Klüver-Bucy syndrome are varied but can include the following:

  • Lack of Fear: Individuals may show no fear of objects or situations that would normally elicit a fear response.
  • Excessive Curiosity: They may display an intense interest in exploring their surroundings, often in a non-directed and inappropriate manner.
  • Memory Impairment: Short-term memory is often significantly affected, leading to an inability to recall recent events.
  • Oral Tendencies: A tendency to put objects in their mouth, even those that are not edible.
  • Hypersexuality: An increased and often inappropriate sexual drive.

 

Cerebellum (Option A): Responsible for motor coordination and balance. Damage → ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor. Does not cause behavioral symptoms like hypersexuality or hyperorality.

Hippocampus (Option C): Critical for forming new memories. Damage → anterograde amnesia. Does not cause hypersexuality or placidity.

Parietal lobe (Option D): Involved in spatial awareness, sensory integration, and body awareness. Damage can cause hemineglect, apraxia, or Gerstmann syndrome. Behavioral disinhibition is not typical.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.solution: >rigidity Explanation: Elevated ammonia crosses the blood–brain barrier and is detoxified to glutamine in astrocytes. Excess glutamine increases osmotic pressure , leading to astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and impaired neurotransmission . Clinical features of ammonia neurotoxicity: CNS dysfunction manifests as tremors, slurred speech, drowsiness, incoordination, visual disturbances , and in severe cases, coma or death . Rigidity involves extrapyramidal/motor pathways , which are not primarily affected by ammonia. Muscle tone is usually preserved in hyperammonemia, helping differentiate it from conditions like Parkinsonism or tetanus. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Rigidity involves extrapyramidal/motor pathways, which are not primarily affected by ammonia.

    • Muscle tone is usually preserved in hyperammonemia, helping differentiate it from conditions like Parkinsonism or tetanus.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old anxious female presents with hyperventilation during a panic attack. ABG shows: pH: 7.48 PaCO2: 20 mmHg HCO3-: 22 mEq/L Which acid-base disorder is present?
questions.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old anxious female presents with hyperventilation during a panic attack. ABG shows:
	pH: 7.48
	PaCO2: 20 mmHg
	HCO3-: 22 mEq/L
Which acid-base disorder is present?
questions.solution: customMeta" data-dictid="cfad80a0f716927771979aae100f95">respiratory alkalosis Explanation: In this case, the patient's panic attack has caused hyperventilation, leading to excessive CO2 washout (low PaCO2 of 30 mmHg, normal is 35-45 mmHg) The elevated pH of 7.48 (above normal 7.35-7.45) confirms alkalosis, while the low PaCO2 identifies it as respiratory in origin. We know that ACUTE : pH increases by 0.08 units and HCO3 decreases by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2 CHRONIC : pH increases by 0.03 units and HCO3 decreases by 5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2 In this patient ABG shows: pH: 7.48 PaCO2: 20 mmHg HCO3-: 20 mEq/L Normal PaCO2 - 38-42 mm hg Thus difference in PaCO2 = 42-22 = 20 mm hg As this patient is having an episode of anxiety attack, it is leading to acute respiratory alkalosis Thus pH should ↑ by 0.08 units and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2 pH should ↑ by 0.008 units and HCO3 ↓ by 0.2 mEq/L per 1 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2 For 20 mm hg fall in PaCO2 pH should ↑ by 0.16 units and HCO3 ↓ by 4 mEq/L (compensated) In this patient pH has ↑ 0.8 and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L (taking 7.40 as normal pH and 22-26 as normal serum HCO3- ) This pattern represents partial compensation because: 1) The pH remains elevated despite some compensation, 2) The HCO3- has started to decrease (compensation has begun), but 3) The compensation isn't enough to normalize the pH. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
customMeta" data-dictid="cfad80a0f716927771979aae100f95">respiratory alkalosis

Explanation:

  • In this case, the patient's panic attack has caused hyperventilation, leading to excessive CO2 washout (low PaCO2 of 30 mmHg, normal is 35-45 mmHg)
  • The elevated pH of 7.48 (above normal 7.35-7.45) confirms alkalosis, while the low PaCO2 identifies it as respiratory in origin.

We know that

  • ACUTE: pH increases by 0.08 units and HCO3 decreases by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2
  • CHRONIC: pH increases by 0.03 units and HCO3 decreases by 5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2
    • In this patient ABG shows:
  • pH: 7.48
  • PaCO2: 20 mmHg
  • HCO3-: 20 mEq/L
  • Normal PaCO2 - 38-42 mm hg

Thus difference in PaCO2 = 42-22 = 20 mm hg

 

As this patient is having an episode of anxiety attack, it is leading to acute respiratory alkalosis

  • Thus pH should ↑ by 0.08 units and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2
  • pH should ↑ by 0.008 units and HCO3 ↓ by 0.2 mEq/L per 1 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2
  • For 20 mm hg fall in PaCO2
    • pH should ↑ by 0.16 units and HCO3 ↓ by 4 mEq/L (compensated)
    • In this patient pH has ↑ 0.8 and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L (taking 7.40 as normal pH and 22-26 as normal serum HCO3- )

This pattern represents partial compensation because:

1) The pH remains elevated despite some compensation,

2) The HCO3- has started to decrease (compensation has begun), but

3) The compensation isn't enough to normalize the pH.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida came for a routine antenatal check at 32 weeks gestation. As the medical officer, which of the following is your responsibility during the antenatal period? A. Antenatal counseling for the mother B. Team briefing and individual responsibility allocation C. Equipment check and preparation D. Proper history taking i.e. prior history of preterm delivery or abortions
questions.stemHtml:
A 24-year-old primigravida came for a routine antenatal check at 32 weeks gestation. As the medical officer, which of the following is your responsibility during the antenatal period?
A. Antenatal counseling for the mother
B. Team briefing and individual responsibility allocation
C. Equipment check and preparation
D. Proper history taking i.e. prior history of preterm delivery or abortions
questions.solution: xplanation: In antenatal care, the medical officer plays a comprehensive role in ensuring both maternal and fetal wellbeing. Each of the listed options represents a valid and essential responsibility during the antenatal period: Antenatal counseling for the mother (Option A): Counselling on nutrition, rest, warning signs, birth preparedness, and family planning is a core component of ANC . Helps in early identification of risk factors and improves compliance with care. Team briefing and individual responsibility allocation (Option B): Although more emphasized in intrapartum care or emergencies , team readiness and role clarity is important throughout pregnancy , especially in high-risk cases. Promotes coordinated care and avoids delay in emergencies. Equipment check and preparation (Option C): Ensures availability of functional equipment for monitoring (BP apparatus, fetal Doppler, weighing scale, etc.) and emergency preparedness . Critical for centres offering delivery services or managing complications. ​​​ Proper history taking (e.g., prior preterm delivery or abortions) (Option D): A comprehensive history helps in risk stratification , planning investigations, and interventions. Past obstetric history is vital for predicting complications in the current pregnancy. Conclusion: Each of these tasks falls under the preventive, promotive, or preparatory functions of antenatal care. @Neet_pg_bot

xplanation:

 

In antenatal care, the medical officer plays a comprehensive role in ensuring both maternal and fetal wellbeing. Each of the listed options represents a valid and essential responsibility during the antenatal period:

Antenatal counseling for the mother (Option A):

  • Helps in early identification of risk factors and improves compliance with care.

Team briefing and individual responsibility allocation (Option B):

  • Although more emphasized in intrapartum care or emergencies, team readiness and role clarity is important throughout pregnancy, especially in high-risk cases.

  • Promotes coordinated care and avoids delay in emergencies.

Equipment check and preparation (Option C):

  • Ensures availability of functional equipment for monitoring (BP apparatus, fetal Doppler, weighing scale, etc.) and emergency preparedness.

  • Critical for centres offering delivery services or managing complications.

​​​Proper history taking (e.g., prior preterm delivery or abortions) (Option D):  

  • A comprehensive history helps in risk stratification, planning investigations, and interventions.

  • Past obstetric history is vital for predicting complications in the current pregnancy.

Conclusion:

Each of these tasks falls under the preventive, promotive, or preparatory functions of antenatal care.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male smoker presents with a persistent cough and mild shortness of breath. Chest imaging reveals a solitary pulmonary nodule. A biopsy is performed, and a histopathological examination of the lung tissue is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male smoker presents with a persistent cough and mild shortness of breath. Chest imaging reveals a solitary pulmonary nodule. A biopsy is performed, and a histopathological examination of the lung tissue is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

questions.solution: localised proliferation of dysplastic cells along pre-existing alveolar septa, indicative of adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) or bronchioloalveolar carcinoma which is a precancerous lesion of adenocarcinoma of the lung with severe cytologic atypia . AIS is an early stage of lung cancer where abnormal glandular cells are confined to the airway lining without invasion and exhibit a “lepidic growth pattern” (or butterfly on fence pattern), spreading along intact alveolar structures without invasion. Lesions are usually small, measuring ≤ 3 cm. Carcinoma in situ (Option A): Carcinoma in situ involves abnormal squamous cells confined to the epithelium without invading the surrounding structures. Adenomatous hyperplasia (Option B): Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH) is a precursor lesion of lung adenocarcinoma with mild cytologic atypia, characterised by dysplastic pneumocytes lining alveolar walls. These lesions are typically small, ≤5 mm , and can be single or multiple. AAH may be adjacent to invasive tumours or independently within the lung tissue and signifies an initial stage in adenocarcinoma development. Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (Option D): DIPNECH (Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia) is a preneoplastic condition characterised by the abnormal proliferation of neuroendocrine cells in the lungs, which can progress to develop into neuroendocrine tumours over time like small cell carcinoma and carcinoid tumours. @Neet_pg_bot

localised proliferation of dysplastic cells along pre-existing alveolar septa, indicative of adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) or bronchioloalveolar carcinoma which is a precancerous lesion of adenocarcinoma of the lung with severe cytologic atypia.
  • AIS is an early stage of lung cancer where abnormal glandular cells are confined to the airway lining without invasion and exhibit a “lepidic growth pattern” (or butterfly on fence pattern), spreading along intact alveolar structures without invasion.
  • Lesions are usually small, measuring ≤ 3 cm.

    • Carcinoma in situ (Option A):

    • Carcinoma in situ involves abnormal squamous cells confined to the epithelium without invading the surrounding structures.

     

    Adenomatous hyperplasia (Option B):

    • Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH) is a precursor lesion of lung adenocarcinoma with mild cytologic atypia, characterised by dysplastic pneumocytes lining alveolar walls.
    • These lesions are typically small, ≤5 mm, and can be single or multiple.
    • AAH may be adjacent to invasive tumours or independently within the lung tissue and signifies an initial stage in adenocarcinoma development.

    Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (Option D):

    • DIPNECH (Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia) is a preneoplastic condition characterised by the abnormal proliferation of neuroendocrine cells in the lungs, which can progress to develop into neuroendocrine tumours over time like small cell carcinoma and carcinoid tumours.
